Summary:

The accused
were charged with four terrorism offences arising from a plot to place pressure
cooker bombs outside the Parliament Buildings in Victoria on Canada Day in
2013. The plot was the culmination of a months-long undercover investigation by
the RCMP. The trial judge directed an acquittal on the count of facilitating a
terrorist activity on the grounds that the accused could not facilitate their
own activity. She also directed the jury that if they convicted the accused of
conspiring to commit murder for a terrorist group, then they were not to
consider another conspiracy count. The jury returned guilty verdicts on the
count of conspiring to commit murder for a terrorist group and on the count of
making or possessing an explosive with intent to endanger life for a terrorist
group. The trial judge entered a stay of proceedings on the other conspiracy
count. The defence then applied for a stay of proceedings on the remaining
counts on the basis that the accused were entrapped by the RCMP. The trial
judge allowed the application and entered stays of proceedings on the final two
counts. The trial judge found entrapment on three bases. First, the trial judge
found that the RCMP provided the accused with an opportunity to commit the
offences without reasonable suspicion that the accused would otherwise commit
an offence. The trial judge found that the RCMP should have realized that the
defendants were not capable of acting on their extremist beliefs when they
committed to provide them with the explosive C-4. Second, the trial judge found
that the average person in the accused’s position would have committed the same
crimes. She found that the RCMP had convinced the accused that they would be
killed if they did not carry out the plot. Finally, she found that the police
conduct exceeded the grounds of propriety and the RCMP effectively manufactured
the crime. The Crown appeals the acquittal, the stay of proceedings on the
conspiracy count, and the stays stemming from entrapment.

Held:
Appeal allowed in part. The acquittal is set aside and a stay of proceedings is
substituted. The remaining appeals are dismissed.

The trial
judge erred in finding that the RCMP lacked reasonable suspicion that the
accused would commit an offence. The trial judge also erred in finding that the
average person would have committed the offences. The conduct of the RCMP could
not have objectively been considered threatening. However, the trial judge did
not err in finding that the conduct of the RCMP satisfied the residual category
of entrapment. The RCMP knew early on that the accused did not have the ability
to commit an act of terrorism. They pushed the accused to create a workable
plan when they were unable to do so on their own. The overall conduct of the
investigation was a travesty of justice and a stay of proceedings must issue.

The trial
judge erred in directing an acquittal on the facilitation count. The accused could
have facilitated each other’s terrorist activity. The acquittal must be set
aside and replaced with a stay of proceedings. The trial judge also erred in
staying the second conspiracy count. The result would be a stay of proceedings in
any event, so this appeal must be dismissed. The terrorism legislation is
unnecessarily complex and cumbersome and should be revisited by Parliament.

Reasons for Judgment of the Honourable Madam Justice Bennett:

A.

Overview

[
1
]

On Canada Day, July 1, 2013, John Nuttall and
Amanda Korody placed pressure cooker bombs outside the Parliament Buildings in
Victoria, B.C. The bombs were timed to explode 15 minutes apart to ensure that
maximum damage would be done to first responders who attended the scene to aid
those harmed by the first explosion. Had the bombs been real, many people would
have died or been injured.

[
2
]

But the bombs were not real and they did not
explode. The minute sliver of explosive substance in the bombs had been
provided by the police, who had participated in the entire scheme. The trial
judge concluded that the police manufactured the crimes and stayed the charges
on the basis of entrapment, despite the jury’s verdict of guilty.

[
3
]

Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody were recent
converts to the Muslim faith. Mr. Nuttall had been attending mosques in
the Lower Mainland, openly espousing violent jihadist views, and looking for
like-minded people. One wonders what would have happened if the police had not
intervened and Mr. Nuttall had actually met someone else with similar
extremist views. Fortunately, and notably, he was consistently rebuffed and his
views repudiated by Muslims who met him in those mosques and prayer rooms.

[
4
]

The couple were charged with four counts of terrorism-related
offences arising from this plot. The trial judge removed one count in relation
to facilitating a terrorist activity from the jury and directed an acquittal.
She also instructed the jury not to consider a second count of conspiracy if
they found the defendants guilty on the first conspiracy count. The jury
convicted both accused of the two remaining counts, and the trial judge entered
a conditional stay of proceedings on the second conspiracy count. The trial
judge also stayed the remaining two counts on the basis of entrapment and abuse
of process. At the same time she imposed an unconditional stay of proceedings
on the second conspiracy count. The Crown appeals the acquittal and the stays
of proceedings in relation to all of the counts.

[
5
]

The entrapment ruling is indexed as
2016 BCSC
1404
(the “Reasons”). In that ruling the judge also stayed the second
conspiracy count. The reasons for the acquittal on the facilitation count are
indexed as
2015 BCSC 943

proceedings on the second conspiracy count are indexed as
2015 BCSC 962
.

[
6
]

I would dismiss the appeals from the stays of
proceedings entered on the basis of entrapment. While, in my view, the trial
judge erred in her analysis on several bases, her ultimate conclusion was
supported by the evidence.

[
7
]

I would dismiss the appeal from the stay of
proceedings on the second conspiracy count and would allow the appeal from the
acquittal to the extent of substituting a stay of proceedings. In my opinion, the
trial judge erred in directing an acquittal on the basis that someone charged
with “facilitat[ing] a terrorist activity” must be external to the terrorist
organization. She also erred in her instruction to the jury on the conspiracy
counts, which had the effect of removing one count from the jury. Nevertheless,
the defence of entrapment would apply to both counts, as would the rule against
multiple convictions.

[
8
]

Throughout these proceedings, in both this Court
and the court below, the word “jihad” has been used synonymously with “Islamic
terrorism”. However, in Islam, jihad is a contested term with a range of
possible meanings. In the
Oxford Encyclopedia of Islam and Politics
(Oxford:
Oxford University Press, 2014) entry for “jihād”, Rudolph Peters and David
Cook explain some of those meanings:

[

sake of Islam and the
ummah

society (“

of the tongue” and “
jihād
of

word means an armed struggle against the unbelievers. Sometimes the “
jihād
of

jihād
,” in opposition to the
peaceful forms named “the greater
jihād
.”

[
9
]

As a matter of clarity, therefore, these reasons
refer to “violent” or “extremist” jihad wherever possible.

The trial judge withdrew count 3 (the “Facilitation
Count”) from the jury, reasoning that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody, as
the alleged principals to the other charged offences, could not “facilitate”
their own terrorist activity. She also instructed the jurors that if they
concluded that the two accused were guilty of count 1 then they were not to
consider count 2, as an accused can only be convicted of one conspiracy arising
from the same delict. As the jury convicted the two accused on count 1, in
accordance with the trial judge’s instructions, it did not return a verdict on count
2.

[

]

The Crown’s grounds of appeal with respect to
the judge’s finding of entrapment substantially relate to alleged palpable and
overriding errors in her factual findings. Thus, it is necessary to delve into

C.

Evidence Leading up to the Charges

[
14
]

The police began investigating Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody as a result of receiving information that Mr. Nuttall
had been openly endorsing violent jihadist views. The team included both
investigative officers and members of the “undercover shop”, comprised of
undercover officers and the cover officers who give them directions. Corporal
A. was the primary undercover officer who interacted with Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody.
Another officer, Constable F., also participated in undercover scenarios. Staff
Sergeant T. was also an undercover officer. Corporal M. was the cover officer.
The Senior Command Officers were Sergeants K., M., and S. Sergeant M. was eventually
replaced by Staff Sergeant K. Sergeant S. participated in later undercover
scenarios as the “brother” who held a senior position in the international
terrorist organization that Corporal A. belonged to. The investigation was
based on 28 scenarios principally involving Corporal A., Mr. Nuttall, and Ms. Korody.

[
15
]

The investigation that led to the charges
against Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody was conducted by the Royal
Canadian Mounted Police (“RCMP”) Integrated National Security Team (“INSET”).
The impetus for the investigation came from information about Mr. Nuttall
collected or obtained by INSET between July 2012 and February 2013 from a number
of different sources:

(a)

A report dated July 5, 2012, from a Surrey RCMP patrol officer. The
report described an incident in which a woman (who was intoxicated when she
spoke with the police) overheard Mr. Nuttall on the street, speaking on a
cellular phone in a loud voice about “the afterlife” and “blowing up” Islamic
countries.

(b)

An initial report and a series of follow-up interviews with M.C.
between October 12, 2012, and February 6, 2013. M.C. met Mr. Nuttall, whom
M.C. knew to be a recent convert to Islam, at a local mosque. Among other
things, M.C. told the police that Mr. Nuttall claimed to have shot a
Jewish woman, and asked M.C. to help him travel to Afghanistan to commit
violent jihad and become a holy warrior. M.C. said Mr. Nuttall had been
asked to leave a prayer room, a Muslim school, and a number of mosques in the
Lower Mainland due to his interest in extremist jihad. After the police
approached Mr. Nuttall to discuss these matters, M.C. reported that Mr. Nuttall
left him phone messages accusing him of being a “traitor to the cause”. He also
expressed concerns about Mr. Nuttall’s mental health.

(c)

Two separate letters from the Canadian Security Intelligence Service
(“CSIS”). On January 16, 2013, INSET received a letter from CSIS reporting that
Mr. Nuttall was a potential threat to national security. This letter was
nothing more than a “tip”; it was unsourced and did not contain any actionable
details. On February 7, 2013, INSET received a more detailed letter from CSIS,
reporting that Mr. Nuttall had recently made attempts to purchase
potassium nitrate—a chemical precursor that can be used to manufacture explosives—from
pharmacies in the Lower Mainland.

At the time, the police were unable
to confirm that Mr. Nuttall had in fact made attempts to acquire this
material, as they did not want to lose the ability to use undercover officers
in their investigation. Later in the investigation, they obtained surveillance
video of Mr. Nuttall’s attendance at a pharmacy on the relevant date,
although Sergeant K. agreed at trial that the video did not advance the
investigation and nothing in the footage corroborated “any effort” to purchase
potassium nitrate. During an undercover scenario, Mr. Nuttall did tell
Corporal A. that he had acquired potassium nitrate from a drug store in the
past.

(d)

Police database queries indicating that Mr. Nuttall had a
criminal record and had been the subject of numerous complaints and
investigations. Mr. Nuttall’s criminal record included: a conviction in
1995 for carrying a concealed weapon; convictions in 1996 for robbery,
kidnapping, and aggravated assault; a conviction in 1997 for assault; a
conviction in 2002 for assault; and a conviction in 2003 for robbery. Mr. Nuttall
had also been the subject of multiple entries in the RCMP’s PRIME database,
including two different 2010 files in which witnesses had reported seeing Mr. Nuttall
use physical violence against Ms. Korody, a 2003 file about Mr. Nuttall’s
involvement in mugging a person, a 2001 report that Mr. Nuttall had
vandalized a pharmacy after the staff refused to fill his methadone
prescription, and a 1995 report indicating that Mr. Nuttall was charged
with attempted murder in relation to the collection of a drug debt. The
databases indicated that Mr. Nuttall had medical and mental health issues
as well as drug dependency.

[
16
]

Between February 2, 2013, and February 23, 2013,
the RCMP conducted surveillance of Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody to
determine their movements and travel patterns. The police determined that Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody lived in a basement suite in Surrey with Mr. Nuttall’s
grandmother. They observed that the two stayed inside their basement suite for
long periods of time. When they left, it was on foot to go to a gas station
store or the grocery store. They did not have a car and both were unemployed
and receiving social assistance. They stayed close to home, rarely leaving a
four-block radius.

[
17
]

The RCMP decided to commence an undercover
project to determine whether Mr. Nuttall was a threat to the public.

[

February 23, 2013 (Scenario 1)
– Corporal A. went to the gas station store where Mr. Nuttall
was seen to buy groceries and snacks, and he exchanged glances with Mr. Nuttall.

[

Corporal A. was subsequently instructed to
pretend he was an Arab businessman who was looking for his niece, who had left

time, his role changed to a wealthy-benefactor-like businessman who had
contacts with those interested in extremist jihad. This new role came into
being after Mr. Nuttall first mentioned violent jihad. Eventually,
Corporal A. was seen as a “trusted friend” and “brother” to Mr. Nuttall.

[

]

March 2, 2013 (Scenario 2)
– Corporal A. went back to the gas station. He had Islamic literature
on his vehicle’s dashboard and a photo of his “niece”. Mr. Nuttall
approached the gas station, and Corporal A. asked him if he could help him
locate his niece. Corporal A. was already aware that Mr. Nuttall had
conservative Islamic religious views, and he explained that his niece fled
their household because she did not want to wear a niqab.

[
21
]

Mr. Nuttall was unguarded about his
extremist jihadist beliefs. The trial judge found that he demonstrated a “naïve,
child-like demeanour”. As soon as he saw the Islamic literature in the car, Mr. Nuttall
told Corporal A. that he was a recent convert to Islam. He told Corporal A.
about things he had read, and was pleased that Corporal A. knew they were
written by Osama bin Laden. Mr. Nuttall told Corporal A. that he was a “mujahid”.
He told Corporal A. that he did not like Canada’s position towards Palestine.
He said that he had plans to travel to Pakistan with a friend to fight violent
jihad, but that they were thwarted when another friend reported him to the police.
He said he had a plan that required money, guns, and equipment that included a
plasma cutter, welding machine and metal sheeting. He said he was not on a
suicide mission, and did not want to kill himself—he wanted to be able to carry
out such plans repeatedly. He said that he did not want to kill women and
children, but that government employees, politicians, and members of the
military were all fair game.

[

]

Mr. Nuttall told Corporal A. that he was
good with electronics and computers. He told Corporal A. that he could hack
into an Israeli government server and cause it to crash. Mr. Nuttall said

[

appeared distrustful of Corporal A., who told Mr. Nuttall that he did not
have to do the job if he did not want to and that the two could remain friends

INSET provided to Mr. Nuttall or Ms. Korody over the course of the

[

The job involved some complicated directions but
Mr. Nuttall apparently completed it without difficulty. He was paid $100.
They went to an Afghan restaurant, where Corporal A. ordered takeout for Mr. Nuttall
to take home to Ms. Korody. While they were waiting for the food to be
prepared, Mr. Nuttall showed Corporal A. videos that inspired him to build
the rockets. He told Corporal A. that he was capable of building one. He showed
Corporal A. videos of Chechen men beheading Russian soldiers. He opened the

cause an enormous blast, and Mr. Nuttall chuckled and praised Allah. He
said he did not regret what he did, and invited Corporal A. to join them in the
hotel room to watch news covering the explosions on television. He estimated
that 200 people would be killed.

[
208
]

When they arrived at the hotel, Corporal A. took the couple to their
room and told them to stay there and not to call him unless it was a real
emergency. Corporal A. left with Mr. Nuttall’s laptop and told him he was
going to destroy it. Mr. Nuttall became agitated when he did not see news
of the blast on TV. He surmised that the news was being suppressed because the
government was afraid it was an al-Qaeda attack, and Ms. Korody agreed. By
11:00 a.m., however, he became very concerned that there was no news of the
blast.

[
209
]

At 11:45 a.m., Corporal A. called and Mr. Nuttall told him the
bombs had not gone off. Corporal A. said that they would get a flight and be
out of the country before 3:00 p.m. When he got off the phone, Mr. Nuttall
was angry, and said the pressure cookers had worked before he handed them off,
so Corporal A. must have done something to them. Ms. Korody agreed. As
they packed, Mr. Nuttall prayed that the devices would still detonate, but
not when children were around.

[
210
]

Corporal A. called back and told them to leave everything behind in
the hotel room except the clothes they were wearing, and that they were to be
transported to an airport. When they stepped into the hallway at 1:50 p.m.,
they were arrested and the operation concluded.

D.

Directed Verdict on the Facilitation Count (
2015
BCSC 943
)

[
211
]

The defence sought a directed verdict at the close of the Crown’s
case, arguing that there was no evidence that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
facilitated a terrorist activity, the offence charged in the Facilitation Count.
The defence submitted that the evidence suggested the accused were the ones who
placed the explosive devices, and that the Crown led no evidence that they
facilitated others within the meaning of s. 83.19 of the
Code
.

[
212
]

Section 83.19 of the
Code
reads:

(1) Every one who knowingly facilitates a
terrorist activity is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to
imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

(2) For the purposes of this Part, a
terrorist activity is facilitated whether or not

(a) the facilitator
knows that a particular terrorist activity is facilitated;

(b) any particular
terrorist activity was foreseen or planned at the time

it was facilitated; or

(c) any terrorist activity was actually carried out.

[
213
]

“Terrorist activity” is defined expansively in s. 83.01 of the
Code
.

[
214
]

The primary defence argument was that the legislative intent of
s. 83.19 of the
Code
demonstrates that the provision should only
apply to persons who helped others to carry out terrorist activities, and that
other sections of the
Code
apply to the principals of those activities.

[
215
]

The Crown submitted that the provision is broad enough to capture
principals of the substantive offence of committing a terrorist activity,
similar to a lesser included offence, which is implicitly part of a greater
offence. The Crown also argued that the definition of “facilitate” is broad
enough to include helping oneself to commit a later terrorist activity and
that, on the facts, Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody’s earlier purchase of
pressure cookers was an act that facilitated their later
“placing of an explosive device…” as captured by count 2. The Crown’s
final argument was that the charge should be left with the jury, and if there
was a question of overlapping convictions, the rule against multiple
convictions as set out
in
R. v. Kienapple

(1974),
1974 CanLII 14 (SCC)
,
[1975] 1 S.C.R. 729
,

could have been applied to stay the Facilitation Count if the jury
delivered guilty verdicts on both counts.

[
216
]

Because the
Code
does not define “facilitation”,
the trial judge turned to case law for a definition. She adopted the definition
developed
in
R. v. Lindsay
,
2009 ONCA 532
, which interpreted the term “facilitation”
in s. 467.1(1) of the
Code
. That provision defines a criminal
organization as a group that has as one of its main purposes or activities “the
facilitation or commission of one or more offences that, if committed, would
likely result in a direct or indirect benefit to the group”. Justice MacPherson
defined “facilitation” in that context as “to make a matter easier”, and as “the
act of making it easier for another person to commit a crime”:
Lindsay

at
paras.
23 and 24
.

[
217
]

The trial judge then looked to statements made by the federal
government before the Special Senate Committee Regarding Bill C-36, which
introduced s. 83.19 of the
Code
. She found that those statements
demonstrated that the provision was intended to target those who could not be
captured by existing party liability law in the
Code
because they did
not know the specific offence that would be committed, but were nonetheless
knowingly facilitating a terrorist activity.

[
218
]

The trial judge also engaged in statutory interpretation of s. 83.19
of the
Code
. She noted that knowledge is an element of the offence, such
that the accused must know that the facilitation is for a terrorist activity.
She reasoned that if Parliament intended s. 83.19 of the
Code
to
apply to principals “who essentially aided themselves in the commission of the
terrorist activity”, the knowledge requirement would be superfluous, as would
the caveat that the facilitator does not have to know whether the activity was
planned at the time of the facilitation, or whether it was actually carried
out.
She held that it was unreasonable to
interpret the act of facilitation as applying “to the acts of a terrorist group
themselves or to the actual participants in the alleged terrorist activity”.

[
219
]

In rejecting the Crown’s argument, the trial judge held that its
broad proposed interpretation of s. 83.19 of the
Code
“[built] in
the spectre of double punishment”, because a principal could be convicted of
the substantive terrorist activity as well as being convicted of knowingly
facilitating the very same activity.

[
220
]

Ultimately, the trial judge determined that the
purpose of s. 83.19 of the
Code
is:

…to capture persons who were on the periphery of
terrorist groups and activities, but nevertheless aided in carrying out the
acts themselves where the Crown could not prove knowledge of the specific
terrorist activity involved. It was not intended to create additional
punishment for the principal offenders who actually commit the terrorist
activity.

[
221
]

The trial judge determined that the conduct
targeted by s. 83.19 of the
Code
was not encompassed by the
evidence led by the Crown and was inconsistent with the theory of liability it
maintained throughout its case. Accordingly, she directed a verdict of not guilty
for both accused on the Facilitation Count.

E.

Ruling on the “Duplicity” of Counts 1 and 2
(
2015 BCSC 962
)

[
222
]

The defence also applied for a ruling that counts 1 and 2 of the
indictment, which both deal with conspiracy, were duplicitous because they both
related to the same agreement and merely represented two objects of the same
conspiracy.

[
223
]

The operative part of count 1 reads that the
couple:

…did conspire
together, the one with the other, to murder persons unknown contrary to
s.465(1)
(a)
of the
Criminal Code
,

for the benefit of, at the direction of, or
in association with a terrorist group…

[
224
]

The Crown did not particularize this count. In its opening address
to the jury, it limited the conspiracy to an agreement between Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody to murder persons unknown by placing the pressure cooker
devices, which the Crown said were explosive, on the grounds of the Parliament
Buildings in Victoria.

[
225
]

The operative part of count 2 reads that the
couple:

…did conspire
together, the one with the other, to commit an indictable offence, to wit:
placing an explosive in or against a place of public use, or a government or
public facility, with intent to cause death or serious bodily injury, contrary
to
s.431.2(2)
of the
Criminal Code
,

for the benefit of, at the direction
or, or in association with a terrorist group…

[
226
]

Similarly, the Crown limited its case on count 2 to a conspiracy to
place the pressure cooker devices on the grounds of the Parliament Buildings in
Victoria, with the intent to cause death, and the additional element of the
intention to cause serious bodily harm, which is an element of s. 431.2(2)
of the
Code
.

[
227
]

The trial judge noted that the sole difference between these two
counts is the object of the conspiracy, in that the second count includes an
intention to cause serious bodily injury as an alternative to an intention to
cause death.

[
228
]

The trial judge observed that where there is only one agreement, but
different illegal objects, there can only be one conspiracy conviction, because
the “substance of the offence of conspiracy to commit an indictable offence is
the agreement and not the commission of the offence”. She noted that where a
single conspiracy has multiple objects, the Crown need only prove one object to
support a conviction.

[
229
]

The trial judge determined that the Crown did
not allege two separate conspiracies in counts 1 and 2, but one conspiracy with
two different unlawful objects. Accordingly, she rejected the Crown’s
submissions regarding
Kienapple
:

In my view,
this is not a potential
Kienapple
situation
where the accused could be convicted of two crimes arising out of the same factual
matrix. Instead, the accused would be convicted of the same crime twice for the
same delict. As a consequence, this is not a situation where the court should
leave the matter to the jury and then address multiple convictions
based
on
Kienapple
after conviction. Instead, the court must
instruct the jury that there is only one conspiracy, and thus they cannot
convict the accused on both counts.

[
230
]

Accordingly, the trial judge determined that if the jury were to
convict on count 1, it should not go on to determine if the couple were guilty
on count 2. She held that she would remedy the duplicity in the counts by
giving an instruction to that effect to the jury. Because the jury ultimately
convicted the accused on count 1, it did not return a verdict on count 2. The
trial judge then entered a conditional stay of proceedings on count 2. She
entered an “unconditional” stay of proceedings at the end of the case as part
of the entrapment ruling.

F.

Ruling on Entrapment and Abuse of Process (
2016 BCSC 1404
)

[
231
]

After the jury returned its guilty verdicts, Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
sought stays of proceedings on the grounds of entrapment and abuse of process.
The trial judge granted a stay of proceedings on the grounds that the police
entrapped the couple. In a separate analysis, she found that police misconduct
during the investigation rose to the level of an abuse of process warranting a
stay.

(1)

Entrapment ruling

[
232
]

At the outset of her legal analysis, the trial judge recognized that

R. v.

Mack
,
1988 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903, was the leading authority on
entrapment in Canadian law. She explained that entrapment is founded on the
need to preserve the integrity of the justice system and is therefore a form of
abuse of process. She found that she could enter a stay of proceedings if entrapment
was made out.

[
233
]

The trial judge wrote that three strands of entrapment were
recognized in
Mack
, all of which, she wrote, required an objective
examination of the police conduct. The first is where the state provides a person
with an opportunity to commit an offence either without acting on a reasonable
suspicion that the person was already engaged in criminal activity or pursuant
to a
bona fide
inquiry. The second is where the police go beyond
providing an opportunity and induce the commission of the offence, such that an
average person with the accused’s “strengths and weaknesses” would have
committed the crime. The third and final category the trial judge recognized is
a residual category of cases in which other factors support a finding of
entrapment.

a.

Launching the investigation

[
234
]

The trial judge found the police had “very little evidence” at the
beginning of the operation to support a reasonable suspicion that Mr. Nuttall
was already engaged in terrorism-related criminal activity. She noted that the
RCMP had no knowledge of the reliability of the CSIS tip regarding Mr. Nuttall
and could not assume it was accurate. The initial surveillance revealed no
evidence that the couple were involved in criminal activity and, indeed, they
did very little outside their home. She noted that, at the time, it was not an
offence to voice support for extremist jihadist beliefs or to travel outside
Canada to carry out violent jihad and that radical beliefs, without more, could
not amount to reasonable suspicion that the couple were already engaged in
criminal activities. However, she concluded that the decision to embark on the
investigation could not be faulted, as infiltrating terrorist groups is an
essential method of investigating terrorism-related offences.

[
235
]

Despite the lack of reasonable suspicion at the commencement of the
operation, the trial judge was satisfied that after the first meeting with
Corporal A., Mr. Nuttall’s openly extremist statements, coupled with his
conduct in the subsequent scenarios, “amply met the objective test for
reasonable suspicion”.

[
236
]

The trial judge acknowledged that distinguishing investigative steps
from the provision of an opportunity to commit the offence required a complex
inquiry, as there were many promises made to the couple that could be
interpreted “as setting the stage for the offer to commit an offence”.

b.

Opportunity to commit the offence

[
237
]

In May and early June, once it was clear that the train plot was
nonsensical due to the lack of a passenger train in Victoria, the investigative
team struggled with whether to end the operation. The trial judge noted that
some officers articulated a concern that the operation was overly influential,
and that the police might turn Mr. Nuttall into a terrorist when he lacked
the capacity to be one on his own.

[
238
]

Of course, the operation continued. The trial judge found that the
offer to provide the defendants C-4, given the context of that offer, constituted
an opportunity to commit the offence. She found that the offer was “held out as
a package deal”, as Corporal A. told the couple that he would not finance any
of Mr. Nuttall’s other schemes because they were unfeasible. She found
that “all of the steps taken by the police after the Kelowna scenarios were
intended to bring this pressure cooker plan, using C-4 as the explosive, to
fruition”.

[
239
]

The trial judge found that Corporal A.’s offer of C-4 on June 16 was
not merely an inquiry into whether the couple were willing to engage in a
terrorist act or any other preliminary investigatory step. She found that it
was “a firm and specific opportunity [to commit an offence]”, whereby Corporal
A. “committed unconditionally to provide [C-4] for the pressure cooker devices”.

c.

Reasonable suspicion that the couple were already engaged in
criminal activity

[
240
]

The trial judge found that Mr. Nuttall’s constant rhetoric of
jihadist violence may have been disturbing, but it was also tiresome because
nothing ever came of those expressions of belief. She found that there was
ample evidence by June 2013 that confirmed Mr. Nuttall’s general
ineptitude, scatterbrained character, inability to think logically, and his
inability to remain focused, which would have been “essential to the
articulation and execution of a terrorist plot”.

[
241
]

The trial judge found that while Mr. Nuttall talked incessantly
about violent jihad, by the time of the Kelowna trip, he had demonstrated the “imaginary
nature of his ideas and a lack of capacity to plan and execute them”. She found
that even Corporal A.’s pointed and repetitive attempts to focus the couple to
form a concrete plan were “singularly unsuccessful in motivating them beyond
talking about their religious beliefs and their jihadist ideas”. She also found
that while there was no doubt that Mr. Nuttall expressed a desire to
obtain a firearm, he did not do anything to further that desire beyond talking
about it.

[
242
]

Apart from outings with Corporal A., the trial judge noted that
surveillance revealed that the couple spent all of their time within a
four-block radius of their suite and never associated with radical individuals
in person or on social media.

[
243
]

In light of these findings, the trial judge concluded that at the
time Corporal A. offered C-4 for the pressure cooker devices, there was “little
objective evidence to support a reasonable suspicion” that the couple were
already engaged in criminal activity related to terrorism. She concluded that
the offer of C-4 amounted to random virtue-testing within the meaning in
Mack
,

based on Sergeant K.’s belief that Mr. Nuttall was predisposed to
violence and that given enough incentive, he would commit a terrorist act.

[
244
]

Ms. Korody did not have any meaningful contact with police
before the May 5, 2013 Whistler trip. Before then, the trial judge noted that
the only police knowledge of her desire to participate in a violent jihadist
plot came from Mr. Nuttall, whom she found to be “a notoriously unreliable
source of information”, such that the police would not have had a reasonable
suspicion that she was already involved in criminal activity based solely on Mr. Nuttall’s
statements about her intentions.

[
245
]

After the May 5 Whistler trip, the trial judge found that it was
apparent that Ms. Korody was complicit in Mr. Nuttall’s grandiose
schemes, providing the police with a reasonable suspicion within the meaning of

Mack

from that point forward. However, as with Mr. Nuttall, the
trial judge found that by mid-June 2013, Ms. Korody had shown no more
capacity to carry out and plan a terrorist act than Mr. Nuttall had.
Accordingly, she also found that the offer of C-4, as it related to Ms. Korody,
amounted to the police’s providing an opportunity to commit a terrorist offence
without a reasonable suspicion that she was already engaged in criminal
activity.

[
246
]

Based on these findings, the trial judge held that the police
entrapped the couple. Accordingly, she entered a stay of proceedings on counts 1
and 4, and an unconditional stay on count 2.

d.

Inducement

[
247
]

The trial judge also considered the second branch of entrapment. The
second branch applies where the police, although they have a reasonable
suspicion that the defendants are involved in criminal activity, go beyond
providing an opportunity and actually induce the commission of the offence:
Mack

at 959.

[
248
]

The trial judge found, in assessing the whole of the operation, that
this was not a situation in which the police disrupted an ongoing criminal
plan, but that the offences were instead “brought about by the police” in a “clear
case of police-manufactured crime”. She assessed the
Mack
inducement
factors in groups, (summarized below) because much of the evidence informed
multiple factors. In the aggregate, the trial judge concluded that “[v]irtually
every one of those factors [was] in play in this case”.

[
249
]

Use of deceit, fraud, and implied threats; no ongoing criminal
venture
: The trial judge found that the police
effort to convince the couple that Corporal A. was part of a large and
sophisticated terrorist organization engaging in international acts of violence
informed these factors. While the couple were “naïve [and] gullible”, she
reasoned that an average person, unburdened by those “personal frailties”,
would probably have come to the same conclusion that the officers were part of
a sophisticated organization that “would not hesitate to eliminate them if they
failed to meet their expectations”. She found it unnecessary for the police to
have resorted to the “extraordinary investigative methods” that they did, considering
Mr. Nuttall’s extreme frankness about his extremist beliefs even upon his
first meeting with Corporal A. Additionally, she reasoned that portraying
Corporal A. as part of a terrorist organization “was not required to maintain
public safety” in light of the lack of an independent threat she found that Mr. Nuttall
posed and that, if anything, “the ruse increased Mr. Nuttall’s excitement
about doing jihad”.

[
250
]

Exploitation of vulnerabilities and friendship
: The trial judge found that the police conduct “involved blatant
manipulation of the defendants to exploit their dependence” upon Corporal A.
and his friendship, citing their reliance on social assistance, their lack of
friends and family support, and their status as recovering heroin addicts. She
found that the couple were highly dependant on Corporal A. “in every respect”,
that he wielded great influence over them, and that he used their attachment to
manipulate their actions. She also found that Corporal A. ensured that Mr. Nuttall
involved Ms. Korody in the operation, dictated the plan that Mr. Nuttall
“had to choose for his jihadist statement and the date and timing of this
mission”, and tricked him into believing that whatever he did was Allah’s will.
Due to their “unsophistication and child-like nature”, the couple came to trust
and love Corporal A. completely, making it easy for him to manipulate them and
to isolate them from outside influences like friends and family.

[
251
]

Police conduct undermining constitutional values
: The trial judge found that Corporal A.’s conduct concerning the
provision of spiritual advice and his repeated rejection of Mr. Nuttall’s
requests to connect with an imam undermined values enshrined in the s. 2(a)

Charter
right of freedom of conscience and religion. While she did not
explore in her entrapment analysis whether Corporal A.’s actions actually
violated s. 2(a), she concluded that “the gravamen of the police
misconduct is the decision to use spiritual guidance to induce a crime that was
motivated by religious beliefs”. She found that the couple did not have a
working knowledge of Islam, and found that Corporal A.’s actions undermined
s. 2(a)
Charter
values by isolating the couple from outside
religious guidance, providing them guidance solely based on introspection and Corporal
A.’s own interpretation of the Quran, and encouraging Mr. Nuttall to only
seek spiritual advice from Corporal A., given that Mr. Nuttall’s
dependence upon the corporal was evident. The trial judge accepted expert
evidence adduced by the couple that by promoting an introspective approach to
Islamic interpretation that advocated “looking into one’s heart”, combined with
Corporal A.’s counsel to adopt an extremist view on the use of violence, the
officer isolated Mr. Nuttall from a moderate viewpoint and “propelled him
toward a more radical conception of jihad”. She found that Corporal A.’s
concept of predestination, which he often offered in response to Mr. Nuttall’s
repeated requests for spiritual advice, encouraged the couple to “put aside
their qualms about killing people because Allah decides everyone’s fate”.

[
252
]

Persistence and proportionality of police conduct, including illegal
acts
: The trial judge found that the police efforts
to “mould” Mr. Nuttall into someone who could execute the pressure cooker
plot were overly persistent and disproportionate to the roles of the accused.
Further, she found that certain police conduct that pushed the operation
forward actually amounted to criminal offences. She found that there was no
evidence that the couple crafted plans to carry out violent jihad while alone,
and that it was only when officers were present that they talked about
committing violent terrorist acts. According to the trial judge, Corporal A.
was persistent in his conduct, which included repeated instructions on how to
craft a plan, redirection away from the couple’s “unfeasible and grandiose”
plans, and pledges to set aside any obstacles, be they financial, technical,
logistical, or religious. She found Mr. Nuttall’s fear of the officers to
be genuine and found that it would have been clear to them that he feared for
his life when he broke down in tears after being confronted with the
impossibility of the passenger train hijacking plan.

[
253
]

To the trial judge, the Victoria recce also amounted to police
manipulation. She found that Corporal A. convinced Mr. Nuttall to go to
Victoria before he had a specific plan, insisted that Ms. Korody attend,
used the trip to expand his fictitious organization by introducing more
officers, impressed the couple with his willingness to finance the trip, and
allayed Mr. Nuttall’s concerns that the plan to commit extremist jihad
would be an affront to Allah.

[
254
]

Finally, the trial judge found that the police role in the mission
violated the
Code
because almost all of their actions relating to
obtaining and handling real C-4 were “unsanctioned”, and beyond the scope of
the s. 25.1
Code
authorization that the RCMP secured at the outset
of the operation. She dealt more fully with these criminal acts in her abuse of
process discussion, but found that the police aided and abetted the couple in
the commission of explosives- and terrorism-related offences under the
Code
.

(2)

Abuse
of process ruling

[
255
]

The trial judge also ruled that the police conduct outlined above
amounted to an abuse of process warranting a stay under the “residual category”,
satisfied where state conduct risks undermining the integrity of the judicial
process:
R. v. Babos
,
2014 SCC 16
at para.
31
.

[
256
]

For this ruling, the trial judge incorporated her entrapment findings—which
related to the couple’s vulnerability and lack of motivation and capacity to
commit the offences on their own—with her findings on the police conduct. She
found that the police conduct in this case was an abuse of process because it
was a “multi-faceted manipulation” of the couple, whom the police exploited
while they were “impoverished, socially isolated and searching for spiritual
meaning in their lives”.

[
257
]

After those general comments, the trial judge analysed what she
identified as illegal acts committed by the police. Based on her analysis of
the meaning of “facilitation” in s. 83.19 of the
Code
,

outlined
above, she found that the police aided and abetted the couple by providing them
with C-4, tools, transportation, accommodation, a location for construction,
technical and logistical advice, and food, which were all “critical to carrying
out the terrorist activity”. She noted that the police were aware of the couple’s
desire to commit terrorist activities, and thus met the
mens rea
requirement
of “knowingly” facilitating those activities. She also ruled that the police
aided and abetted the offence of making or having an explosive substance with
intent, for the benefit of, in association with, or at the direction of a
terrorist group under ss. 81(1)(d) and 83.2 of the
Code
. She noted
that all of the elements of that offence were made out in respect of the
principals (Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody) based on the jury verdict.
The trial judge found that the police had knowledge of the couple’s intent to
make use of an explosive device to cause death and property destruction at the
Parliament Buildings, and acted intentionally to assist them in carrying out
that plan. She found that the police did not obtain the requisite authorization
under s. 25.1 of the
Code
to use actual C-4 in the undercover
operation, and that “[t]he law does not accord the police a general
justification defence for engaging in criminal acts, even where they go
undercover to investigate illegal activities”.

[
258
]

She found that the police essentially treated the operation like a
traditional Mr. Big investigation. However, the key difference she
identified was that unlike post-offence assistance offered to a suspect to
facilitate a Mr. Big investigation, “where the object of the investigation
is to facilitate the offence, albeit in a controlled manner, the police cannot
break the law with impunity unless they have authorization to do so under
s. 25.1”.

[
259
]

The trial judge concluded that the police conduct, although “egregious”
for the purposes of the entrapment inquiry, did not interfere with the couple’s
freedom of conscience and religion in a non-trivial way. This was because
although Corporal A. promoted certain religious beliefs and disparaged others, “[i]nducing
a particular religious belief…is not a state-imposed limitation on the
defendants’ freedom to choose their own religious beliefs”.

[
260
]

The trial judge ruled that the police conduct amounted to an abuse
of process warranting a stay of proceedings. While she did not make a finding
that the police acted in bad faith, she found a need to curtail police action “in
a prospective sense” to ensure that future investigations did not follow the
same path, and found that to permit the convictions to stand in the face of
this kind of misconduct would cause irreparable damage to the integrity of the
justice system.

G.

Issues on the Appeals

[
261
]

There are two separate Crown appeals in relation to each respondent.
The first relates to the trial judge’s entrapment ruling, under which the Crown
raises several issues. First, it says that there were many palpable and
overriding errors in the trial judge’s factual findings. Second, it says that
she erred in law in finding that the police no longer had “reasonable suspicion”
when they offered to buy C-4 explosives. Third, it says that the trial judge
lost sight of the fact that one of the counts was a conspiracy charge, and that
their ability to carry through with the act of building and placing the bombs
was not dispositive of the offence. Fourth, and finally, it says that she was
incorrect to conclude that the police conduct amounted to an abuse of process requiring
that the two remaining counts be stayed.

[
262
]

The second appeal alleges two primary errors. They are procedurally
and substantively distinct enough that I refer to them as separate appeals throughout
these reasons. The first relates to the decision of the trial judge to direct a
verdict of acquittal on the Facilitation Count, finding that members of
terrorist organizations cannot facilitate their own terrorist acts. The second
relates to the instruction to the jury on the two conspiracy counts, which
essentially took count 2 away from the jury.

H.

Crown Right to Appeal

[
263
]

The Crown appeals the acquittal on the
Facilitation Count, the stay of proceedings on count 2, and the stay of
proceedings on counts 1 and 4. The Crown’s right to appeal the acquittal is
found in s. 676(1)(a) of the
Code
, and its right to appeal the stays
of proceedings is provided by s. 676(1)(c):

676

(1)
The Attorney General or counsel instructed by him for the purpose
may appeal to the court of appeal

(a)
against a judgment or verdict of acquittal or a verdict of not
criminally responsible on account of mental disorder of a trial court in
proceedings by indictment on any ground of appeal that involves a question of
law alone;

…

(c)
against
an order of a trial court that stays proceedings on an indictment or quashes an
indictment; …

[
264
]

On an appeal from an acquittal under s. 676(1)(a), the Crown is
limited to questions of law alone. By contrast, when the appeal is from a stay
of proceedings under s. 676(1)(c), the Crown can appeal on the basis of
law, fact, or mixed fact and law:
R. v. Franc
,
2016 SKCA 129
at para.
25
;

R. v. Nguyen
,
2013 ONCA 169
at para.
46
.

I.

Standards of Review

(1)

Questions of fact

[
265
]

Findings of fact cannot be reversed on appeal
unless it can be demonstrated that the trial judge made a “palpable and
overriding error”:
Housen v. Nikolaisen
,
2002 SCC 33
. The standard “employ[s]
a high level of appellate deference to findings of fact” and will only be met
when a finding is “clearly wrong”:
Housen
at paras.
10 and 22
.

[
266
]

At para. 14 of
Housen
, Justice
Iacobucci and Justice Major quoted Robert D. Gibbens’s article “Appellate
Review of Findings of Fact” (1991–2) 13 Advocates’ Q 445 at 446:

The trial judge is said to have an expertise
in assessing and weighing the facts developed at trial. Similarly, the trial
judge has also been exposed to the entire case. The trial judge has sat through
the entire case and his ultimate judgment reflects this total familiarity with
the evidence. The insight gained by the trial judge who has lived with the case
for several days, weeks or even months may be far deeper than that of the Court
of Appeal whose view of the case is much more limited and narrow, often being
shaped and distorted by the various orders or rulings being challenged.

[
267
]

The test of palpable and overriding error applies to both findings
of fact and inferences of fact:
Housen
at paras.
10 and 19
.

[
268
]

In
Benhaim v. St-Germain
,
2016 SCC 48
,
Wagner J. (as he then was) quoted Stratas J.A. and Morissette J.A. in his review
of the meaning of palpable and overriding error:

[38]

It is equally
useful to recall what is meant by “palpable and overriding error”. Stratas J.A.
described the deferential standard as follows in
South Yukon Forest Corp. v.
R.
,
2012 FCA 165
, 4 B.L.R. (5th) 31, at para.
46
:

Palpable and
overriding error is a highly deferential standard of review . . . . “Palpable”
means an error that is obvious. “Overriding” means an error that goes to the
very core of the outcome of the case. When arguing palpable and overriding
error, it is not enough to pull at leaves and branches and leave the tree
standing. The entire tree must fall.

[39]

Or, as Morissette
J.A. put it in
J.G. v. Nadeau
,
2016 QCCA 167
, at para.
77
(CanLII), [
translation]

“
a palpable and
overriding error is in the nature not of a needle in a haystack, but of a beam
in the eye
. And it is impossible to confuse these last two notions.”

[Emphasis added.]

[
269
]

To state it simply, a palpable and overriding error is an obvious
error that erodes the result.

[
270
]

In
H.L. v. Canada
,

2005 SCC 25
,
Justice Fish discussed alternative formulations of the “palpable and overriding
error” standard. He explained that such an error is “clearly wrong” in that the
appellate court can plainly identify the imputed error and show how it affected
the result: at para. 55. He wrote that the test is also met when the
findings of fact are “unreasonable or unsupported by the evidence”: at para. 56.
That language is more familiar to the criminal law, which permits an appeal on
that basis under s. 686(1)(a)(i) of the
Code
. In criminal law, this
provision does not apply to an appeal from an acquittal, as an “unreasonable
acquittal” is incompatible with the presumption of innocence and the burden of
proof on the Crown:
R. v. Biniaris
,
2000 SCC 15
at para.
33
, citing

Schuldt v. The Queen
,
1985 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 592 at 610.

[
271
]

Justice Fish, in
H.L.
at para.
57
, relied
on Prof. Adrian A.S. Zuckerman’s explanation of the standard of review in England
in
Civil Procedure
(London: LexisNexis UK, 2003) at 765–68:

As a general principle, an appeal court must
not interfere with findings of fact made by the lower court for the simple
reason that the judge who saw and heard the witnesses is better placed to
assess their reliability and draw inferences from their testimony. An appeal
court will interfere only if it concludes that no reasonable court could have
reached such conclusions, or if the lower court failed to take crucial factors
into consideration. . . .

. . . It follows that, if the appeal
court cannot conclude that the lower court’s inference from the primary facts
was wrong, in the sense that it fell outside the range of inferences that a reasonable
court could make, the appeal court should allow the lower court’s decision to
stand. The nature of the appellate evaluation of the lower court’s decision
will vary in accordance with the type of judgment that the lower court was
called upon to make. But whatever the nature of the issues and however wide or
narrow is the room for disagreement, the test remains the same: was the lower
court’s decision wrong. . . .

A decision will be
wrong if it was founded on an incorrect interpretation of statute, or if it
wrongly applied a legal principle, or if it was based on a plainly erroneous
factual conclusion. . . . Put another way, as long as the lower court’s
conclusions represent a reasonable inference from the facts, the appeal court
must not interfere with its decision.

[
272
]

I note that the weighing of evidence is not a question of law alone,
but an absence of evidence to support a finding is a question of law alone:
Schuldt

at 610.

(2)

Stays of proceedings

[
273
]

The standard of review from a stay of
proceedings is also deferential. Justice LeBel framed the standard in
R. v.
Regan
,
2002 SCC 12
:

[117]

The decision to grant a stay is a discretionary one, which should not
be lightly interfered with: “an appellate court will be justified in
intervening in a trial judge’s exercise of his discretion only if the trial
judge misdirects himself or if his decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to
an injustice” (
Tobiass
, [
1997 CanLII 322 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 391] at para. 87;
Elsom

v.

Elsom
,
1989 CanLII 100 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1367, at p. 1375). Furthermore,
where a trial judge exercises her or his discretion, that decision cannot be
replaced simply because the appellate court has a different assessment of the
facts (
Stein

v.

The Ship “Kathy K”
,
1975 CanLII 146 (SCC)
, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802;
see also
R
.
v.

Oickle
, [2000] 2 S.C.R. 3,
2000 SCC 38
;
R
.

v.

Van der Peet
,
1996 CanLII 216 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 507).

[118]

This does not mean, however, that the trial judge is completely
insulated from review. It is settled law that where the “trial judge made some
palpable and overriding error which affected his assessment of the facts”, the
decision based on these facts may be reversed (
Kathy K
, at p. 808)…

[
274
]

In
Regan
, LeBel J. concluded that “the trial judge made palpable
and overriding factual errors which set his assessment of the facts askew” (at para. 118).
He also concluded that the trial judge erred in law by misdirecting himself
regarding the law for granting a stay of proceedings (at para. 121).

[
275
]

Recently, in
Babos
, Justice Moldaver, for
the majority, reiterated the standard of review from a stay of proceedings:

[48]      The standard of review for a remedy
ordered under s. 24(1) of the
Charter
is well established. Appellate
intervention is warranted only where a trial judge misdirects him or herself in
law, commits a reviewable error of fact, or renders a decision that is “so
clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice” (
Bellusci
, at para. 19;

Regan
, at para.
117
;
Tobiass
, at para.
87
;
R. v.
Bjelland
,

2009 SCC 38
, [2009] 2 S.C.R. 651, at paras.
15 and
51
)

(3)

Questions of law

[
276
]

Finally, questions of law are reviewed on a correctness standard:
Housen

at para.
8
. No deference is owed to the trial judge’s findings on
questions of law.

J.

Entrapment

[
277
]

As has been oft quoted, “the investigation of crime and the
detection of criminals is not a game to be governed by the Marquess of
Queensbury rules” (
R. v. Rothman
,
1981 CanLII 23 (SCC)
, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 640 at 697, per Lamer
J.). However, while criminal investigations may not be models of politeness and
fair play, they are not “no holds barred”. There are still rules. Justice Lamer
(as he then was), in
Mack
, outlined when those rules will be broken and
when the “ends do not justify the means” (at 938).

[
278
]

Early steps towards establishing entrapment as a viable aspect of
the abuse of process doctrine, now enshrined in s. 7 (
R. v. O’Connor
,

1995 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 411 at paras.
70–71
), were taken in the concurring decision
of Chief Justice Laskin in
Kirzner v. The Queen
,
1977 CanLII 38 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 487 at
492–94.
Kirzner
was a drug trafficking case in which the defence of
entrapment was taken from the jury at trial. The decision was upheld on appeal.
The Ontario Court of Appeal had concluded that no such “defence” existed. In
the Supreme Court, the majority concluded that the evidence did not support
entrapment and dismissed the appeal without considering if the defence existed.
The minority also dismissed the appeal on the same basis, but explored the
possibility of such a defence, leaving the question open for another time. The
minority acknowledged that so-called “consensual crimes”—crimes involving
willing persons—including gambling and drug trafficking, do not necessarily
lend themselves to “ordinary methods of detection” (at 493). Chief Justice Laskin
isolated the judicial concern where the police have gone beyond “mere
solicitation or mere decoy work and have actively organized a scheme of
ensnarement, of entrapment, in order to prosecute the person so caught” (at 494).
He discussed the disparate approaches in the United States, where the dichotomy
was a “subjective approach” which relied on the predisposition of the offender,
or an “objective approach” which focused on the conduct of the police (at 494).
Although Laskin C.J.C. raised the issues, he left the answers to another day
and another case (at 498).

[
279
]

As we know, in
Mack
, the Court came down squarely in favour
of an objective approach.

[
280
]

The issue was next raised in the Supreme Court
in
Amato v. The Queen
,
1982 CanLII 31 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 418. In
Amato
, another drug
trafficking case, the majority concluded that if the defence existed, it did
not arise on the facts presented. Justice Estey’s dissent, which ultimately
formed the foundation of the defence in
Mack
, discussed the issue at
length and concluded that the defence did exist. It concluded that the police
conduct was “shocking and outrageous” and that the defence applied in the facts
of that case. The dissent also pointed out that although entrapment is called a
“defence”, it is not a true defence, as it does not justify or excuse
behaviour.

[
281
]

Justice Estey explained that for some offences,
including those involving violence, entrapment would usually be inapplicable.
He wrote that it would most frequently arise for the “consensual offences” that
Laskin C.J.C. referenced in
Kirzner
, such as drug trafficking and
illegal gambling. Justice Estey wrote that “[p]olicing must react differently
to this kind of crime” and, significantly, that “[t]he move from passive to
active policing brings the courts into the process” (at 457). When policing was
purely “passive”, the police and courts filled familiar roles and addressed
familiar problems: the police gathered evidence and made arrests, and the
courts determined the admissibility of that evidence and the guilt or innocence
of those arrested and charged by applying legal principles. With “active”
policing came new issues (at 458):

The appointed spy
may, pursuant to arrangements, infiltrate and report upon participants in a
crime to which the agent may be a party or which the agent has provided to
others the opportunity to commit. In some circumstances, indeed, the offence
would in all likelihood not have otherwise been committed. The law enforcement
agency in these circumstances moves from the position of merely affording an
opportunity for the commission of crime to persons who may be so disposed to a
position where the agency itself encourages the commission of the crime.
Expressed another way, the police may have by any such measures instigated the
offence, or at least its planning, and did so simply to catch the otherwise
innocent members of the public in order to prosecute them. The ensnared or
entrapped must in such a situation have a defence in law for the police and the
state have gone beyond mere crime detection by decoy work or solicitation of
evidence. In fact the crime has been designed and committed by the state
itself.

[
282
]

I turn now to
Mack
, where the Court unanimously embraced the
existence of the “defence” of entrapment. In
Mack
, the accused resisted
approaches by a police informer over a number of months in regard to drug
trafficking. He testified that he eventually capitulated to the requests
because of the use of threats and the inducement of a large amount of money.

[
283
]

In
Mack
, Lamer J. identified the “ubiquitous nature of
criminal activity in our society” (at 916) and acknowledged that many crimes
are committed in secret and are of a consensual nature. He also identified
where the dividing line is between acceptable and unacceptable police conduct.
That distinction is between the police’s providing an opportunity to a person
to commit an offence while acting on “reasonable suspicion” or in the “course
of a
bona fide
inquiry”, and “the state actually creating a crime for
the purpose of prosecution” (at 917).

[
284
]

Justice Lamer explained, following Estey J.’s dissent in
Amato
,
that entrapment is an aspect of the abuse of process doctrine. It allows a
court to enter a stay of proceedings “in circumstances where allowing the
accused to stand trial would offend the courts’ sense of justice” (at 919).

[
285
]

The rationale for entrapment is the maintenance of the integrity of
our court system. As Lamer J. found, “It is a deeply ingrained value in our
democratic system that the ends do not justify the means” (at 938).
Significantly, this means that recognizing entrapment is not a matter of a
court inappropriately disciplining the police (at 942). The court instead invokes
its legitimate power to stay the proceedings because to condone the state’s
conduct would be to sacrifice the integrity of the administration of justice.

[
286
]

Justice Lamer recognized that there are competing interests at play
in the doctrine of entrapment. We do not accept police conduct that amounts to
entrapment because there must be inherent limits on the way that state power
can be wielded to “attain…the specific objective of obtaining convictions” (at
941). He wrote that the “intuitive reaction” against entrapment arises from a
constellation of overlapping concerns, including that the techniques may result
in the commission of crimes by people who otherwise would not have committed
them, and that the police should not engage in criminal conduct for the purpose
of entrapping others. He identified the latter concern as engaging the rule of
law: creating crime is an inappropriate use of the substantial powers that we
afford the police.

[
287
]

On the other hand, Lamer J. recognized that repressing criminal
activity is an important social interest. Crime brings great costs to individuals
and society at large. We depend on the police to protect us from those costs.
What is required, Lamer J. explained, is “balance between the concepts of
fairness and justice and the need for protection from crime” (at 942).

[
288
]

Reviewing, once again, the debate on whether the focus is on the
subjective state of mind of the accused or the objective conduct of the police,
Lamer J. concluded that the predisposition and subjective state of mind of the
accused is not the issue. The focus is on the
objective conduct of the
police
, and whether the police acted improperly (at 954–55).

[
289
]

Justice Lamer concluded that entrapment will exist when: (a) the police provide an individual with the opportunity to commit an
offence without reasonable suspicion or while acting
mala fides
, or (b) although
they have a reasonable suspicion or are acting in the course of a
bona fide

inquiry, they go beyond providing an opportunity and actually induce the
commission of an offence (at 959).

[
290
]

Justice Lamer said that in assessing whether the
conduct of the police gave rise to the latter category of entrapment (at 959–60):

… it is useful to
consider whether the conduct of the police would have induced the average
person in the position of the accused, i.e., a person with both strengths and
weaknesses, into committing the crime. I believe such a test is useful not only
as an analytical mechanism that is consistent with objective analysis, but also
because it corresponds to one of the reasons why the defence is thought
desirable. In other words, it may be inevitable that, when apprised of the
factual context of an entrapment case, members of the community will put
themselves in the position of the accused; if a common response would be that
anyone could have been induced by such conduct, this is a valuable sign that
the police have exceeded the bounds of propriety. The reasoning does not go so
far as to imply that the accused is therefore less blameworthy; rather, it
suggests that the state is involved in the
manufacture
as
opposed to the detection of crime.

[Emphasis in original.]

[
291
]

However, Lamer J. also found that the hypothetical or average person
model is not the only relevant method of analysis in the latter category. In
some cases, even if the hypothetical person would not likely have committed the
offence, the conduct of the police can nevertheless support the conclusion that
they went beyond the bounds of propriety and instigated the crime. In such
cases, the police conduct would thereby amount to an abuse of process (at 961–62).

[
292
]

Justice Lamer summarized some of the factors to be
considered in an entrapment analysis as follows (at 966):

−

the type of crime being investigated and the
availability of other techniques for the police detection of its commission;

−

whether an average person, with both strengths
and weaknesses, in the position of the accused would be induced into the commission
of a crime;

−

the persistence and number of attempts made by the
police before the accused agreed to committing the offence;

−

the type of inducement used by the police
including: deceit, fraud, trickery or reward;

−

the timing of the police conduct, in particular
whether the police have instigated the offence or became involved in ongoing
criminal activity;

−

whether the police conduct involves an exploitation
of human characteristics such as the emotions of compassion, sympathy and
friendship;

−

whether the police appear to have exploited a
particular vulnerability of a person such as a mental handicap or a substance
addiction;

−

the proportionality between the police
involvement, as compared to the accused, including an assessment of the degree
of harm caused or risked by the police, as compared to the accused, and the
commission of any illegal acts by the police themselves;

−

the existence of any threats, implied or
express, made to the accused by the police or their agents;

−

whether the police conduct is directed at
undermining other constitutional values.

[
293
]

In summary, Lamer J. identified the rationale for entrapment as the
recognition that there must be inherent limits on state power to “manipulate
people and events” to obtain convictions (at 917). However, this recognition
must be balanced against the competing social interest in the state’s ability
to protect the public from “the immense social and personal cost of crime”.

[
294
]

The guilt or innocence of the accused is not the issue in an
entrapment claim. Entrapment is not a defence; in most cases, police conduct
caught by the doctrine will not have the effect of negating either the
actus
reus
or
mens rea
of the offence:
Mack

at 941 and 943. Rather,
the central issue on an entrapment claim is the “avoidance of the improper
invocation by the state of the judicial process and its powers” (
Mack
at
942, quoting
Amato
at 461, per Estey J., dissenting). In the context of
entrapment, “the court’s sense of justice is offended by the spectacle of an
accused’s being convicted of an offence which is the work of the state”:
Mack

at 942, citing
Amato

at 447, per

Estey J., dissenting.

[
295
]

The Crown must first discharge its burden to prove the essential
elements of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt before an entrapment claim is
heard, and the accused’s guilt or innocence must be determined apart from
evidence relevant only to the issue of entrapment:
Mack

at 972.

[
296
]

Once in the entrapment phase of the proceedings, the onus is on the
accused to prove on a balance of probabilities “that the conduct of the state
is an abuse of process because of entrapment”:
Mack

at 975. As I discuss
further below, if the accused is successful in meeting that burden, then the
remedy is a stay of proceedings.

[
297
]

Entrapment is a question to be the decided by
the trial judge. Justice Lamer identifies the question as “one of law, or mixed
law and fact”:
Mack

at 967. He does not address the standard of
appellate review for entrapment claims. However, in applying the entrapment
principles developed earlier in the reasons, Lamer J. identifies an error in
the trial judge’s reasoning process that could be characterized as an
extricable legal error reviewable for correctness (at 977):

In determining whether
the doctrine of entrapment applies to the present appeal, this Court is
restricted to the summary of evidence provided by Wetmore Co. Ct. J. in his
reasons. I am of the view that a stay of proceedings should be entered in this
case.
While the trial judge had the advantage of hearing the testimony of
the appellant, and normally findings on entrapment cases should not be
disturbed because of this, I am concerned that in this case too much emphasis
was placed on the appellant’s state of mind
. Earlier in my summary of the
decisions below I cited a passage from the trial judge’s reasons wherein he
stated that the fundamental issue was the appellant’s state of mind and his
predisposition to crime. This, perhaps, explains why in his conclusion the
trial judge stated the appellant was not entrapped because he acted out of a desire
to profit from the transaction. If the trial judge had been permitted only to
evaluate the conduct of the police objectively, I think he might well have, and
in any event, ought to have come to the conclusion the police conduct amounted
to entrapment.

[Emphasis added.]

[
298
]

In concluding, the Court emphasized that the burden is on the
offender to establish that theirs is one of the “clearest of cases” of
entrapment, the standard that must be met to establish a stay of proceedings as
a remedy for an abuse of process. Furthermore, “the state must be given
substantial room to develop techniques which assist in its fight against crime
in society” (at 976).

[
299
]

One of the main issues in this case concerns the “reasonable
suspicion” branch of the defence. This Court, in
R. v. Gingras
,
2013
BCCA 293
, concluded that a reasonable suspicion could arise from an accused’s
offers to be involved in criminal activity. This Court, at para. 26,
applied the decision in
R. v. Kang-Brown
,
2008 SCC 18
at para.
75
,
and concluded that the police were not required to operate at a level of
certainty. Reasonable suspicion is something more than a mere suspicion but less
than reasonable and probable grounds.

(1)

Alleged
palpable and overriding errors of fact

[
300
]

The law on entrapment requires careful attention to the facts. If
facts material to the foundation of an entrapment finding are set aside, the
conclusion may be in jeopardy.

[
301
]

The appellant Crown alleges that the trial judge committed a wide
range of palpable and overriding errors in the extensive factual findings
underpinning her entrapment analysis. Most of the trial judge’s factual
findings functionally mirror the factual summary she delivered in her jury
charge, outlined above. Accordingly, here I will set out only those specific
factual findings the Crown impugns on appeal.

[
302
]

The Crown categorizes the alleged factual errors into five main
areas: the impetus for the pressure cooker bomb plot, the timing of the
pressure cooker bomb plot, the placement of the bombs, the construction and
functionality of the bombs, and the respondents’ fear that they would be killed
if they did not follow through with the plot. The positions of the parties are set
out in each section, along with the discussion regarding palpable and
overriding error.

[
303
]

For the reasons that follow, I find that the vast majority of the
trial judge’s factual findings are devoid of palpable and overriding error. The
only exception is the final area: the trial judge’s finding that the
respondents feared that they would be killed was inconsistent with an earlier
finding she made in the course of the trial. Additionally, she applied a
subjective test to those findings. For those reasons, that finding cannot
stand.

a.

Impetus for the pressure cooker bomb plot

[
304
]

The trial judge’s ultimate conclusion on this
point was that the police “instigated and skilfully engineered the very
terrorist act committed by the defendants” (Reasons at para. 718).

[
305
]

The Crown’s position is that Mr. Nuttall first proposed the
plan on April 26, based on a schematic he obtained online from
Inspire

magazine. Mr. Nuttall repeatedly stated his desire to emulate the Boston bombers.
Ms. Korody declared “this is our plan” and “we actually got the idea from,
uh, from the brothers in Boston”.

[
306
]

The defence position is that the fact that Mr. Nuttall was the
first party to mention a pressure cooker plot does not lead, logically or
causatively, to the conclusion that the RCMP did not later redirect him to the
pressure cooker plot, and were not its impetus. The Crown cites Mr. Nuttall’s
brief mention on April 26 of pressure cookers used in the Boston bombing as
proof that the impetus for the ultimate plan was his. However, while Mr. Nuttall
mentioned pressure cookers, the defence submits that he did not commit to that
plan on April 26. He also spoke about other plans, like hijacking a nuclear submarine,
and said nothing about pressure cookers for many weeks afterward (Reasons at para. 170).

[
307
]

The trial judge made the following seven impugned factual findings
driving her conclusion that the police, not Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody,
came up with the pressure cooker bomb plot. The Crown submits that the
conclusion that the police instigated and skillfully engineered the terrorist
attack lies in the following unfounded findings. For the reasons below, I do
not think any of the seven factual findings impugned by the Crown in this
category were palpable and overriding errors. I would not interfere with the
trial judge’s findings on any of the alleged errors.

(i)

When the police realized they could not watch
over Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody indefinitely, they had to “redirect Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody’s jihadist plans towards something that was feasible and
realistic and which could be accomplished quickly and cheaply; namely, the
pressure cooker devices” (Reasons at para. 724).

[
308
]

The Crown’s position is that Mr. Nuttall first raised the
possibility of a pressure cooker bomb attack, and repeatedly characterized it
as a quick, cheap, effective means of pursuing violent jihad. The Crown notes
that Mr. Nuttall said he wanted to proceed as soon as possible because Ms. Korody
was very sick.

[
309
]

The defence says the trial judge acknowledged the police did not
first identify the pressure cooker plot; however, Mr. Nuttall regarded the
device as a tester when he mentioned it, and “the police seized on this idea
and it became their plan” (Reasons at para. 775). The defence notes that Mr. Nuttall
was not referring to the pressure cooker plan when he said he wanted to proceed
as soon as possible.

[
310
]

In my view, this finding by the trial judge was not an error, and was
amply supported by the evidence. The pressure was on the police to wind up the
undercover operation. Mr. Nuttall had been discussing far-fetched plans,
such as launching Qassam rockets, charging the Esquimalt naval base, and taking
possession of a nuclear submarine. The police concluded that they would steer,
and in fact pressured, Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody toward the pressure
cooker bomb plan.

(ii)

“
Shortly after the Boston bombing in mid-April 2013, Mr. Nuttall
commented that the pressure cooker devices used by the Boston bombers was a
good, simple plan. However, he had made no further reference to pressure cookers
until the meeting on June 6th”
(Reasons at para. 734).

[
311
]

The Crown says this is an error because Mr. Nuttall also
repeatedly referred to the Boston bombing as “cheaper”, “easy to do”, and “faster”
than his proposed rocket plan.

[
312
]

The defence position is that even accepting the Crown’s submissions,
this disparity does not amount to a palpable and overriding error of fact.
Additionally, this evidence was more thoroughly reviewed at paras. 170–73
of her reasons, where the trial judge found that on April 26, 2013, Corporal A.
redirected Mr. Nuttall from a discussion of Ms. Korody’s health by
saying that Corporal A. “understood why [Mr. Nuttall was] looking … for an
operation that [could] be done easily, fast, and [wouldn’t] need that much
money” (Reasons at para. 172). The trial judge noted that “[n]one of these
assertions came from Mr. Nuttall”. The defence also says there was
evidence that Mr. Nuttall never said the bomb plot was cheaper, easier to
do, or faster. In cross-examination, it was put to Corporal A. that those words
referred to a totally different plan concerning a train. It was open to the
trial judge to conclude that “fast” and “cheap” were not used to describe the
pressure cookers.

[
313
]

In my view, the conclusion by the trial judge is not an error. There
was no specific mention of the pressure cooker bombs between when Mr. Nuttall
first mentioned them on April 26 and when he showed Corporal A. the
instructions he found in
Inspire
on June 6. I agree with the defence that
it was open to the trial judge to conclude that “fast” and “cheap” were in
reference to one of Mr. Nuttall’s other plans.

(iii)

Prior to June 6, 2013, Mr. Nuttall refused
to use the Internet at home to research his terrorist plans because he was
afraid of detection, and Corporal A. instructed him about Tor anonymity software
to solve the problem (Reasons at para. 734).

[
314
]

The Crown says this is an error because a search of Mr. Nuttall’s
computer revealed he first downloaded the bomb schematic from
Inspire
two
months before meeting Corporal A.

[
315
]

The defence says that the trial judge was making a finding on the
discrete matter of Mr. Nuttall using the Internet for research
at his
own home
. The defence says there was no evidence that when Mr. Nuttall
downloaded
Inspire
two months before meeting Corporal A., he did so
at
his home
, so the trial judge did not err.

[
316
]

Again, the finding that Mr. Nuttall did not download
