information at home before he learned of Tor is supported by the evidence. On
March 7, he told Corporal A. that he did not download anything from extremist
jihadist websites while at home, but only did so using public Wi-Fi hotspots. Corporal
A. told him about Tor during the May 15 scenario.

(iv)

“Mr. Nuttall
presented the pressure cooker diagram to [Corporal
A.] as a means of testing his ability to make an explosive device in
preparation for building the rockets. They were for a tester and ‘not the real
thing’”
(Reasons at para. 734).

[
317
]

The Crown submits that this is an error because Mr. Nuttall also
said, in the same meeting on June 6, “we could do the rocket idea, which I
think is brilliant, but would take a year of planning”; by contrast, the
pressure cooker bomb would not be “as spectacular”, but “the body count [would]
be the same”; it would be “pure terrorism”
.
When Corporal A. asked what Mr. Nuttall
would be doing if they had never met, Mr. Nuttall said he would be making
the kettle bomb “right now”.

[
318
]

The defence argues that Mr. Nuttall described the pressure
cookers as “just for testing, playing around with and you know, practice”. The
defence says it was open to the trial judge to conclude on that date he
described the pressure cooker as a tester. In ensuing scenarios, Mr. Nuttall
described a variety of plans without mentioning pressure cookers (Reasons at para. 320).

[
319
]

In my view, the trial judge’s finding is not an error. While Mr. Nuttall
did tell Corporal A. he would be making a bomb if they never met, the missing
context is that immediately afterward, Mr. Nuttall rambled on about a
number of different plans. The Crown also ignores the trial judge’s analysis of
the events of June 6 and her findings regarding the broader context of the
meeting (Reasons at paras. 318–21, 626–27).

(v)

Mr. Nuttall, Ms. Korody, and
undercover officers discussed the non-feasibility of Mr. Nuttall’s plan to
storm a naval base or launch homemade rockets. The trial judge described Mr. Nuttall’s
“extremely downcast demeanor and tone of voice” in a subsequent interaction
between him and Mr. Korody, in which he told her that “their rocket plan
had to be put aside in favour of [Corporal A.]’s plan that they build pressure
cooker devices, ‘Not [as] a test but the real thing’” (Reasons at para. 739).

[
320
]

The Crown submits that this finding is an error
because after expressing a belief that they were taking resources away from the
mujahideen, Mr. Nuttall’s exact words were:

No we’re not doing that idea anymore. We’re
doing the Boston idea. We’re continue, we’re going to continue their work
*inshallah* okay. That’s what this is about okay. Forget the rockets.
*lnshallah* one day afterwards but we’ve got to continue their work those two
brothers. I see that now, seriously. Look at it like you’re continuing those
brothers work. They got caught they can’t continue.

[
321
]

The defence says notwithstanding that the precise words “not as a
test but the real thing” were not spoken by Mr. Nuttall, the trial judge
accurately captures the thrust of the conversation the Crown quotes. The trial
judge further held that “it was clear that they had gotten the message that their
rocket plan be scrapped in favour of [Corporal A.]’s pressure cooker plan”
(Reasons at para. 346). The defence says that the reference to “real thing”
versus “tester” should be considered in light of the fact that those terms, in
relation to pressure cookers, arose elsewhere in the judgment, reflecting that
these two potential uses of pressure cookers were a repeated theme (Reasons at paras. 319,
627 and 734).

[
322
]

In my view, although the evidence, like Mr. Nuttall’s “plan”,
was “all over the map”, it was open to the trial judge to conclude that Mr. Nuttall’s
initial idea was to use the pressure cooker bomb as a “test” before he
constructed his rockets.

(vi)

After acknowledging that “[t]he police did not
first identify the idea of exploding pressure cookers,” the trial judge added, “however,
Mr. Nuttall regarded this device as a tester” (Reasons at para. 775).

[
323
]

The Crown submits that this is an error because after showing the
bomb diagram to Corporal A., Mr. Nuttall described it as a “tester”, but
in the same June 6 conversation posited that it represented a quicker yet
equally effective alternative to his rocket plan, as his rocket plan would take
a year. In a later conversation, Mr. Nuttall again referred to the bomb as
a “tester”, but said he wanted to make at least four bombs. Mr. Nuttall
purchased four pressure cookers, intending to use one as a tester and the
others as real bombs. Mr. Nuttall later returned one, as it had plastic
hinges and would not explode. When Mr. Nuttall recognized there was no
time for a test, he settled on three pressure cooker bombs, one with its own
timer, and the other two linked together with one timer.

[
324
]

The defence position is that the Crown cites evidence from the last
few days of the operation. Simply because by the end of the operation Mr. Nuttall
no longer viewed the pressure cooker bombs as “testers”, it does not follow
that he did not view them as testers much earlier on, before he was pressured
to adopt the plan.

[
325
]

In my view, the trial judge did not make a palpable and overriding
error. She was correct that Mr. Nuttall considered the pressure cooker
bombs to be testers for much of the investigation. Further, Mr. Nuttall
again mentioned a number of different plans in a short period of time during
the June 6 conversation with Corporal A. It was open to the trial judge to make
the finding that she did.

(vii)

“At no time did Mr. Nuttall refer to the pressure cookers as
his plan for jihad” (Reasons at para. 734).

[
326
]

The Crown says that this finding is in error because Mr. Nuttall
repeatedly stated that he got the idea from
Inspire
magazine and that he
wanted to “continue” or “build on” the work of the Boston Marathon bombers. Mr. Nuttall
elsewhere stated it was “kind of all our plans”, and “we all kinda chipped in”,
but also said he was “inspired by
Inspire
” and the Boston bombers. Mr. Nuttall
begged Sergeant S. to give him the explosives so he could complete the mission.
Mr. Nuttall described the pressure cooker bombs as his “back up idea”,
conceding that his other ideas were no longer possible, or were less feasible. Ms. Korody
said at various times, “We actually got the idea” from “the brothers in Boston”,
credited Mr. Nuttall for coming up with the idea, and stated, “This is our
plan”.

[
327
]

The defence argues that far from taking ownership of the pressure
cooker plan, Mr. Nuttall identified Corporal A. as the impetus for the
plan. It was only in response to Sergeant S. feigning an angry outburst that Mr. Nuttall
“cast off his diffidence regarding the pressure cooker plot”. The defence says
the interview with Sergeant S. fully supports the trial judge’s findings (Reasons
at paras. 412–20, 734).

[
328
]

In my view, while Mr. Nuttall may not have said the precise
words as found by the trial judge, he clearly, from time to time, took credit
for the plan as his own. On the other hand, the evidence could also support a
finding that the pressure cooker bombs were not Mr. Nuttall’s plan until
much later into the undercover operation, after he was pressured by the police
to follow through with the pressure cooker bombs. Read charitably in context,
the trial judge’s finding is that Mr. Nuttall did not take ownership of
the pressure cooker bomb idea until later in the investigation, after he had
been pressured by the undercover officers to do so. Given that there is
evidence that supports the trial judge’s finding, I cannot interfere with it.

b.

Timing of the pressure cooker bomb plot

[
329
]

The trial judge ultimately concluded that the RCMP dictated the date
and time of the pressure cooker plan (Reasons at para. 692).

[
330
]

The Crown submits that the trial judge made five palpable and
overriding errors in her factual findings related to police direction on the
timing of the plot. I do not agree that any of those findings were palpable and
overriding errors.

(i)

“
The
Victoria recce evidenced the police manipulation of the defendants in several
ways. First, [Corporal A.] manipulated Mr. Nuttall into going to Victoria
before he had decided on a specific plan or selected a target”
(Reasons at para. 729).

[
331
]

The Crown submits that this finding is an error. The Crown relies on
evidence that it says shows that “Mr. Nuttall consistently and repeatedly
affirmed his desire to conduct a terrorist attack on a target in the Victoria
area”. This included evidence that Mr. Nuttall described Victoria as “familiar”
and “easier”, said that the Parliament Buildings were “always” the target, and
said that he “picked” Victoria because he and Ms. Korody knew the city
well.

[
332
]

The Crown also refers to a number of other facts in support of its
contention. Mr. Nuttall first proposed to scout Victoria on May 5, 2013. On
May 10, Corporal A. told Mr. Nuttall he needed to research his plan. Mr. Nuttall
responded that he needed to conduct a recce of potential targets in Victoria
and he wanted to go some time that week. On May 14, Mr. Nuttall, of his
own initiative, bought a digital camera to use for the recce in Victoria,
telling Corporal A. that using the camera to photograph potential terror
targets would amount to “conspiring to commit high treason”. On May 15, 2013, Corporal
A.’s handlers told him to discuss Mr. Nuttall’s wish to conduct a recce. The
Crown submits that it was only then that Corporal A. and Mr. Nuttall began
discussing the logistics of the trip.

[
333
]

The defence asserts that the Crown is advancing a straw man
argument. The defence says that the Crown is not attacking the trial judge’s actual
finding—that the RCMP manipulated the timing of the recce—but what are actually
findings the trial judge did not make regarding manipulation unrelated to timing.

[
334
]

The defence first summarizes evidence supporting the trial judge’s
finding that the RCMP manipulated the Victoria recce timing. On May 10, Mr. Nuttall
spoke to Corporal A. about conducting a recce in Victoria “that week”. Corporal
A. replied that Mr. Nuttall needed to make a plan before that could
happen. The planning the Crown cites was a condition precedent to the recce
occurring. On May 15, Corporal A. asked Mr. Nuttall when he wanted to do
his first recce, and Mr. Nuttall said, “When do you think I should [do]
it? …I need help”. Corporal A. said he would “take care of it”, “let me plan
it, check what I can do”, and later “let me plan it and check when we can go”.
At a May 15 RCMP briefing, investigators discussed whether the Victoria recce
should occur before any plan had crystallized (Reasons at para. 240).

[
335
]

Mr. Nuttall lost enthusiasm as the recce approached and did not
do any of the required planning. On May 22, Corporal A. pressed Mr. Nuttall
to work on targets. Mr. Nuttall said they should defer the recce,
expressing logistical concerns. Corporal A. told Mr. Nuttall not to worry
and that he would take care of it, which Mr. Nuttall agreed to (Reasons at
para. 261).

[
336
]

Turning to the evidence the Crown cites, the defence says the
extracts relate to matters unrelated to the factual finding regarding
manipulation
of timing
. The defence says the Crown cites evidence that makes no
reference to the Victoria recce, and cites numerous references to instances
where Mr. Nuttall discussed targeting Vancouver Island, but says nothing
about whether the RCMP manipulated the timing of the recce. The defence points
to three Crown citations of Mr. Nuttall “repeatedly affirming” his desire
to attack Victoria on June 30, well after the recce occurred. In any event, the
defence submits, the RCMP were interested in a Victoria recce before Mr. Nuttall
ever raised it, as it was raised at an internal meeting on April 9 (Reasons at para. 148).

[
337
]

In my view, this finding is not a palpable and overriding error. On
May 22, Mr. Nuttall thought they were getting ahead of themselves. He
thought they should buy the rockets first because the targets could change. In
addition, I accept the defence’s point that the trial judge’s finding was not
that the police manipulated the target, but that they manipulated the timing of
the recce to Victoria, a finding supported by evidence.

(ii)

“
[Corporal A.] pressured the defendants to come up with a date
for the explosion. He cornered them into a date before Ramadan by saying that
he was going away for this holiday and did not know if he would be coming back
to Canada after Ramadan. [Corporal A.] raised the question of Canada Day…”
(Reasons at para. 374).

[
338
]

The Crown asserts that this finding is an error because Corporal A. did
not propose Canada Day to Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody. In a private
conversation intercepted by the police on or about June 22, 2013, Ms. Korody
said to Mr. Nuttall that they should target a fireworks festival like
Canada Day or B.C. Day. On June 25, 2013, the topic of Canada Day arose after Corporal
A. explained he would be going away for Ramadan, and Mr. Nuttall said they
should get started right away.

[
339
]

The defence says that the finding is justified because the RCMP were
planning from early on that the mission would take place on Canada Day. On June
4, Sergeant K. anticipated Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody would settle in
July 1. On June 5, the RCMP discussed an arrest date of July 1.

On June
16, Ms. Korody said the mission should not occur until after Ramadan. Mr. Nuttall
said it would take a year to plan. Corporal A. said, “The sooner the better,
why take a year?” The investigative plan for the June 25 scenario was to
manipulate Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody into selecting July 1 without
explicitly mentioning it: “[Staff Sergeant K.] would like them to confirm that
July 1st is the day, given it’s Canada Day and before Ramadan. However, this
has to come from the targets”. After Corporal A. said he was leaving for
Ramadan and did not know if he would be coming back, Mr. Nuttall replied, “We
gotta do it before uh ...” Corporal A. said, “If you wanna do it before, when
you gonna do it? Do you have a, a date, like a day that will be like s-, like
significant in mind. Something, I don’t know.” Nuttall continued to demur: “Let’s
get this tested, built… and see, see what this does first.” Corporal A. returned
to the matter of timing in the meeting, and said, “The only thing is, like if
we project a date, then we know how fast we have to work,” and reminded Mr. Nuttall
that the “brother” was on his way. Mr. Nuttall told Corporal A. he thought
it was a mistake to rush. Corporal A. asked what the best time to do it was. Mr. Nuttall
responded that they could do it during one of the fireworks celebrations, going
on to note, “Canada Day is coming up, didn’t you say?” Mr. Nuttall identified
that day as June 1. Ms. Korody clarified it was July 1 and did not know if
5 days was enough time to prepare. Mr. Nuttall asserted they had a month
to prepare, Ms. Korody reminded him it was in five days, and Mr. Nuttall
replied, “It doesn’t have to be July 1st. It’d be nice if it could be July 1st.”
Corporal A. interjected, “No, we can make it…. we can try.” Ms. Korody
said there was another fireworks display August 1. Corporal A. said he would be
away, but said, “Let’s work”, as if they could “make it” for July 1. Corporal
A. pressured them to come up with a mission date within the short time remaining
before he left Canada, and to select a “significant” day. Corporal A. had
previously told Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody that Ramadan began on July
10. The defence submits that the trial judge had ample evidence to find that Corporal
A. manipulated them into choosing Canada Day without mentioning the date
explicitly (Reasons at para. 372).

[
340
]

In my view, it is clear that the police were pushing for Canada Day.
They wanted the operation to conclude, and when Canada Day was mentioned as one
of several dates, the police landed on it, and put the pressure on them to
complete the act on that date. I would not interfere with the trial judge’s
finding.

(iii)

On June 25, when Ms. Korody reminded Mr. Nuttall that
Canada Day was July 1, he felt this was too rushed and wanted to wait until the
following year (Reasons at paras. 374 and 476).

[
341
]

The Crown submits that during the June 25 discussion in which Canada
Day was identified as the day of the attack, Mr. Nuttall did not state he
wanted to wait until the following year. He said they all had to “work hard”.
The Crown submits that in the June 29 interview with Sergeant K., Mr. Nuttall
told him it was his idea to carry out the plan on Canada Day.

[
342
]

The defence submits that the finding is not an error, as Sergeant K.
testified that a wiretap intercept of Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody’s
basement suite showed they were discussing whether to do it Canada Day 2013 or
2014, and whether the timeline was too rushed. The defence submits that the
Crown’s reliance on the interview with Sergeant S. is misplaced, as things Mr. Nuttall
said on June 29 could not inform his words or feelings on June 25. If what Mr. Nuttall
said on June 29 is material, the defence submits the key point is that he
thought the timing was rushed.

[
343
]

On that day, Corporal A. said he thought July 1 was Mr. Nuttall’s
idea, and Mr. Nuttall responded, “No, no, no, it was your idea, brother.” Mr. Nuttall
only changed his tune after Sergeant S. stormed out of the motel room and
erupted in anger. Even then, Mr. Nuttall maintained that Corporal A. had
pressured the timing: “That part is because he has an engagement coming up he
has to meet.” Sergeant S. responded, “Before July 9th.” Mr. Nuttall replied,
“Yes. So, we have to do it before then ... so, why not on Canada Day?” Mr. Nuttall
agreed Canada Day was his idea, but it was Corporal A’s idea to “speed it up
because he’s gotta go.”

[
344
]

In my view, there was evidence to support the trial judge’s finding,
as the defence submits, and it therefore cannot be said that there was a
palpable and overriding error.

(iv)

After the June 25 discussion about Canada Day, Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
felt rushed and wanted to wait until the following year for Canada Day 2014 (Reasons
at paras. 374 and 746).

[
345
]

The Crown says that this finding is an error because Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody agreed they were rushed and would prefer more time if it
was available, but in their private conversations after June 25, they confirmed
they were working toward a deadline less than one week away. Mr. Nuttall and
Ms. Korody expressed both privately and to Corporal A. that the mission
could not wait, and that Canada Day was a good, symbolic day for the bombing.

[
346
]

The defence says that this alleged error is duplicative of the
previous one, and, in any case, the couple continued to feel rushed after the
June 25 meeting. The trial judge found that Staff Sergeant K. directed Corporal
M. that July 1st was the preferred date. He wanted Corporal A. to put pressure
on Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody to accept that date. Corporal M. testified
that investigators believed July 1 was a significant day, and that if Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody had this as their “D Day”, it would spur them on (Reasons
at paras. 371–72). The next day, after Corporal A. discussed Canada Day
with them, Mr. Nuttall asked, “Isn’t Monday gonna be Canada Day?” and
said, “I don’t wanna rush this”. On June 27, Mr. Nuttall told Ms. Korody
he was still uncertain which day Canada Day was. The trial judge relied on
these communications about timing (Reasons at para. 374). On June 30, Mr. Nuttall
continued to talk about the plan being rushed and said that the plan was “forced
on them”.

[
347
]

Although I do not agree that this alleged error is duplicative of
the previous one, I do not think it is a palpable and overriding error. The
previous alleged error concerned the respondents’ state of mind
during

the June 25 meeting, whereas this alleged error concerns the trial judge’s
findings on their state of mind
after
that meeting. In any case, it is
not a palpable and overriding error. As the defence outlines, there was
evidence that supported the trial judge’s conclusion.

(v)

“
It was also [Corporal
A.] who determined when the detonators would be set to go off. He instructed the
defendants when they were going to plant the devices; and that they would plant
the devices and be off the Island before the explosion occurred” (Reasons at para. 757).

[
348
]

The Crown says the evidence shows that the respondents determined
when the devices would be planted. On June 25, Mr. Nuttall first proposed
to plant the bombs at 4:00 or 5:00 a.m., when it was dark, so they could “take
their time” planting the bombs. Ms. Korody said they could set the timers
to give themselves enough time to be off the Island by the time the bombs went
off.

[
349
]

The defence submits that the Crown is relying on decontextualized
pieces of conversations on June 25. The defence says that no decision regarding
timing can be said to have made here, as the very next day, June 26, Mr. Nuttall
told Corporal A. they should plant the bombs at 10:01 a.m. The defence submits
that what Mr. Nuttall said was “the same random scattergun expression of
views that characterized the entire undercover operation”. By June 29, an
objective of that day’s RCMP scenario was to confirm that the bombs would be
placed by 5:00 a.m. This would have been redundant, the defence says, if timing
had already been conclusively determined by Mr. Nuttall. Corporal A. told Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody “…Because five o’clock everything has to be done…. And that’s
my plan. Like that’s what I was working on…” On June 30, Corporal A. told Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody that the devices would be planted at 5:00 a.m. because
there would be few police on the streets. On the alleged error regarding when
the bombs would go off, the defence says Corporal A. told Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
on multiple occasions that the plan would allow them to escape and that it was
not a suicide mission.

[
350
]

In my view, while there was evidence to support another finding, as
the Crown submits, there was evidence supporting the finding of the trial
judge. It cannot be said that she made a palpable and overriding error.

c.

Placement of the bombs

[
351
]

The ultimate finding that the trial judge made on this point was that
the RCMP pressured the respondents into agreeing to a target of the RCMP’s
choosing.

[
352
]

The Crown submits that the trial judge made 11 palpable and
overriding errors relating to her findings that the police directed the
placement of the bombs. In my view, all 11 of those impugned findings were open
on the evidence, and therefore none can be disturbed.

(i)

“
Instead of letting the defendants
direct the timing of any mission, the police used [Corporal A.]’s influence
over them to pressure them into agreeing to a target, a target that the
defendants realized right away was acceptable to [Corporal A.] because he had
pointed it out several times and called it a perfect location for the devices
”
(Reasons at para. 463).

[
353
]

The Crown says that from the outset, Mr. Nuttall proposed the Parliament
Buildings as a potential target. The Crown also points to other evidence that
suggests that the couple took a leading role in choosing the location of the
mission. On June 25, 2013, when Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody settled on
Canada Day for the bombing, Mr. Nuttall said he wanted to reconnoitre
proposed targets when they arrived in Victoria—Corporal A. asked, “Where are
you gonna put ‘em?” and Mr. Nuttall replied, “That’s why we need the
recce.” When building the bombs, Mr. Nuttall told Ms. Korody to
research and develop a list of targets to be checked out during the recce. When
Corporal A. drove Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody to various sites during the
recce, Mr. Nuttall selected possible locations and Corporal A. acted “as
nothing more than a sounding board”.

[
354
]

The defence points to evidence that Ms. Korody’s written list
of targets did not mention the Parliament Buildings.

Ms. Korody’s target
list was given to Sergeant S. on June 30, 2013. The defence says this means when
Corporal A. drove the couple around Victoria on June 30, the Parliament
Buildings were not among their potential targets. The trial judge found that
the first thing Mr. Nuttall asked Corporal A. on the recce was “what was
going to happen now”, and that Corporal A. “was the leader of the group who
instructed his foot soldiers what to do and how to do it.” She found that Corporal

e.

The couple’s fear they would be killed if they did not carry out the
plot

[
395
]

The trial judge’s ultimate conclusion was that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
believed they had to follow through with their plan or would be killed. She
expressed this conclusion in a number of ways: “they would surely be killed” (Reasons

[
396
]

with her findings of fact in the ruling in relation to self-defence.

]

air of reality to the self-defence claim, the trial judge held that there was

reality because there was:

•

No evidence of an express or implied threat to Mr. Nuttall
or Ms. Korody’s safety;

•

No evidence of imminence of any alleged threat,
particularly considering the many available avenues of escape (they had full
access to their cellphones and could freely leave their motel and hotel rooms);
and

•

A lack of proportionality between the alleged
threats and Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody’s willingness to continue
their involvement in a gravely serious plot to place explosive devices in a
place where they could kill and harm many people.

[
398
]

Accordingly, the Crown says this Court should not defer to the trial

[
399
]

a duress analysis” and makes the “specious argument that since there was no

[
400
]

findings related to the couples’ fear that Corporal A. or his associates would

(i)

The trial judge dismissed the officers’ repeated
suggestions that the couple could withdraw from the plan as “standard outs” (Reasons

[
401
]

violent jihadists, there is no evidence they would harm Muslims who refused to

[
402
]

[
403
]

and Ms. Korody also provide context for the opportunities to withdraw. On

[

]

[

]

the Crown says the trial judge was correct in stating that “a decision to place

,
2015 BCSC 963
, at paras.
42–43
). The Crown

(ii)

“
It was in this context that Mr. Nuttall cautioned Ms. Korody

[

]

suggested going to the police but decided against it because it would be “devastating”

[
409
]

Concluding on why this Court should not defer to the trial judge’s
entrapment findings, the Crown says that it was not open to revisit Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody’s “moral involuntariness” to commit the offences and reach
differing conclusions on the entrapment ruling in a manner inconsistent with her
ruling that self-defence lacked an air of reality.

(i)

Discussion

[
410
]

The trial judge had previously been asked to
leave the defence of self-defence with the jury, arguing that the new
Code

provisions, particularly, s. 34(1), expanded the scope of self-defence such
that it was available on the facts of this case. The defence did not seek to
have the defence of duress placed before the jury, recognizing, no doubt, its
inapplicability. The trial judge, in reasons indexed as
2015 BCSC 963
, rejected
the defence argument, concluding that the new provisions had not been expanded
or altered to the extent that the defence argued. However, she continued, and
concluded that if she was wrong in her legal analysis, she would also reject
the defence based on finding that it lacked an air of reality. She said:

[40]      In my view, there is
no
evidence that there is a reasonable underpinning for any subjective belief in Mr. Nuttall
or Ms. Korody that they faced either the use of force or they faced a
threat of force.
While the persona adopted by the undercover police
officers would have led any reasonable person in the accused’s circumstances to
believe they were working with very dangerous people,
nothing that the
officers did or said could have reasonably led the accused to believe that
anyone was using force against them or was threatening force against them at
the time of the events. At its highest, the evidence indicates that the accused
believed they had gone too far with the undercover officers to back out. There
is no evidence of a threat hanging over their heads, either expressly or
implicitly. Ms. Korody in particular believed that she could go home at
any time before leaving Victoria, and it was only Mr. Nuttall’s statements
to her that led her to believe that she could not turn back after that point.

[41]

The defence also lacks an evidentiary foundation because the accused
had time and opportunity to extricate themselves from the situation. They
talked about getting lost in Victoria because they knew the city so well. They
talked about calling the police. They had full access to their cellular
telephones, and while they may have suspected they were being watched, in fact Ms. Korody
left the hotel room in Sydney on her own for a cigarette break, and the accused
also left the motel in Delta on their own and demonstrated no fear of doing so.

[42]

Lastly, there is no proportionality between the accused’s response
and the nature of the threat.
As I indicated earlier, there is no evidence
of a physical threat, there is only evidence that the accused believed the
undercover officers were dangerous and might kill them
. Without an actual
threat to measure its significance, and without any sense of imminence to an
actual or perceived threat, it cannot be said that a decision to place
explosive devices in a public place where they could potentially kill and
injure numerous people is a proportionate response. It is certainly well beyond
what could reasonably be regarded as a proportionate response in the
circumstances.

[43]

In light of the many avenues of escape, as opposed to going ahead
with the plan to place the explosive devices in a public place thereby
endangering others’ lives, as well as the uncertainty of any threat or
perceived threat and the disproportionate nature of the response, I find a
properly instructed jury, acting reasonably, could not acquit the accused on
the basis of self‑defence.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
411
]

These reasons show that the police did and said nothing that would
have led Mr. Nuttall or Ms. Korody to believe that they would be
killed if they did not complete the terrorist act.

[
412
]

Even if at some point Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody
subjectively feared that they would be killed, the evidence is clear that they
did not place the bombs because they feared for their lives; they placed the
bombs because they wanted to do violent jihad. On the day of the attack, Mr. Nuttall
told Corporal A. that he wanted to “do [terrorist acts] forever”.

[
413
]

The defence submits that there was a much greater record before the
judge on the entrapment hearing, which is true. However, they point to no
specific evidence that changes what was actually said by the police to Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody. Nor do they explain how the additional evidence they do
cite can affect the analysis on this point. As noted above, all of that
evidence is contained in audio and video recordings.

[
414
]

The judge’s finding that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody felt
that they would “surely be killed” cannot be upheld. It is inconsistent with the
findings of fact she made on the self-defence ruling, and is clearly not
supported by the evidence, which depicts the couple actively considering escape
and deciding to go through with the plan for reasons other than fear.

[
415
]

In any event, as a matter of law, what is relevant in entrapment is
not Mr. Nuttall’s and Ms. Korody’s subjective beliefs, but the
conduct of the police, considered objectively. Recall that in
Mack
, the
trial judge committed an extricable legal error that was reviewed by the
Supreme Court of Canada on a correctness standard. In this case, the trial
judge’s focus on the accused’s subjective beliefs was incorrect in law. As
found by the trial judge and supported by the evidence, the police did and said
nothing to lead either of the two respondents to reasonably (or otherwise)
believe that they would be killed or harmed if they did not carry out the
planned attack; indeed, the police provided the respondents with a total of 36
opportunities to withdraw between them. They did not take those opportunities.
Objectively, the police could not have made it clearer that the respondents
could withdraw from the plan.

[
416
]

In my view, the trial judge erred in concluding that there was any
conduct by the police that contributed to a belief in certain death or harm,
and thereby erred in including that factor in her analysis on entrapment. I
will address the effect of this finding later in these reasons, in my
discussion of whether the average person in Mr. Nuttall’s and Ms. Korody’s
position would have committed the offences.

(2)

Finding
that the police “lost” their basis for reasonable suspicion that Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody were involved in criminal activity

[
417
]

The trial judge found entrapment on three bases. The first,
discussed at paras. 615–660 of her reasons, was that the police provided
the respondents with the opportunity to commit an offence without reasonable
suspicion that they were already involved in criminal activity when they
offered to provide Mr. Nuttall with C-4 on June 16, 2013.

[
418
]

The Crown submits that the trial judge erred in finding that
offering the C-4 presented the respondents with an “opportunity” to commit an
offence, and that she also erred in finding that when the police presented that
alleged opportunity, they no longer had a reasonable suspicion that the two
were already engaged in criminal activity.

[
419
]

I agree with the Crown that the police had reasonable suspicion that
Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody were involved in criminal activity at the
time the C-4 was offered. In order for this branch of entrapment to be made
out, the defence must show that the police both provided an opportunity to
commit an offence
and
lacked reasonable suspicion at the time they did
so. Given my conclusion on reasonable suspicion, there is no need to consider
whether offering to provide C-4 constituted the presentation of an opportunity.

[
420
]

The trial judge concluded that when the RCMP
offered Mr. Nuttall C-4 on June 16, 2013, they did not have a reasonable
suspicion that he and Ms. Korody were engaged in criminal activity:

[648]    …
at the time the offer of [C-4] was made for the pressure cooker devices, there
was little objective evidence to support a reasonable suspicion that Mr. Nuttall
was already engaged in criminal activity related to terrorism. As Lamer J. said
in
Mack
,
there must be a temporal connection to establish
reasonable suspicion; events that are too remote cannot justify the objective
test. Similarly, suspicions that have been allayed by more recent events cannot
be ignored. It is the sum total of the objective facts that must be
scrutinized, including evidence that supports a conclusion that the defendants
were not otherwise engaged in the planning or execution of terrorist acts.

[649]    Realistically,
the defendants had proven themselves to be marginalized, isolated people who
espoused extremist jihadist views but were neither motivated to act on their
beliefs nor capable of taking steps to accomplish acts of violence in support
of their beliefs. Some of the officers involved in Project Souvenir appeared to
hold this view of the defendants and advocated a different course of action
than the one spearheaded by [Sergeant K.]

[
421
]

However, she also found that Sergeant K.’s decision to present the opportunity
to the accused was based on his belief that Mr. Nuttall was predisposed to
commit a terrorist act, and that given enough incentive, he would do so (at para. 650).
She found that this was not a sufficient basis based on
Mack
and thereby
concluded that the RCMP’s conduct amounted to random-virtue testing.

[
422
]

In my view, the trial judge erred in reaching the conclusion that
when the offer of the C-4 was made the police no longer had a reasonable
suspicion that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody were already engaged in
criminal activity. In
Gingras
, this Court held that proposing to commit
a criminal offence would “[p]resumptively” provide the police with reasonable
suspicion (at para. 25). The trial judge failed to consider Mr. Nuttall’s
conduct in the days prior to the offer of the C-4.

[
423
]

On June 6, 2013,

Corporal A. picked up Mr. Nuttall
outside his residence. Mr. Nuttall had, on his own initiative, downloaded
instructions onto his computer on how to build a homemade explosive device. Mr. Nuttall
had also found information on how to build a pressure cooker bomb in
Inspire

and gave Corporal A. a drawing and math formulas. The instructions, according
to Mr. Nuttall, were the same as the Tsarnaev brothers used. Mr. Nuttall
said that if it worked for them, it could work for him. He also showed Corporal
A. a one-page shopping list with the items he needed in order to build the

he could make C-4. Corporal A. said he was working on getting him C-4. Mr. Nuttall
then spoke about building a model rocket that would explode. Mr. Nuttall
talked about a big plan that would produce a body count like 9/11 to cause
people to rethink sending troops overseas to kill Muslims. Corporal A. asked Mr. Nuttall
what he would be doing if they had not met, and Mr. Nuttall said he would
be making a kettle bomb. Mr. Nuttall wanted to shop for bomb-making parts
right away, but Corporal A. stalled him.

[
424
]

In my view, this evidence alone provided sufficient basis for a
finding of reasonable suspicion. However, there was more. On June 8, Mr. Nuttall
called Corporal A. and said that he had found a natural substance that could be
used as an explosive. On June 9, Mr. Nuttall told Corporal A. that he was
talking about cow manure. Mr. Nuttall said that the recipe looked easy.

[
425
]

Mr. Nuttall was still actively planning a terrorist act. Ms. Korody
was not as engaged as Mr. Nuttall; however, she was clear in her desire to
participate in the terrorist acts discussed.

[
426
]

In my view, the trial judge erred in her conclusion that Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody were entrapped on the basis that the police lacked a
reasonable suspicion that they were involved in criminal activity. The conduct
of both offenders went beyond predisposition, but entered the realm of an
objective suspicion that they may well participate in a terrorist act.

[
427
]

That conclusion is not the end of the matter, however, as the trial
judge also found entrapment based on the second branch of the entrapment test,
and found a distinct abuse of process, both of which, in her view, justified
the stay of proceedings.

(3)

Finding
that a reasonable or average person would have committed the offences

[
428
]

The trial judge concluded, at paras. 769–75 of her reasons, that
the average person would have committed the crimes, and even if the average

[
429
]

The trial judge made the following findings:

•

The police knowingly exploited the demonstrated
vulnerabilities of the defendants in order to induce them to commit the
offences;

•

The police adopted a multi-faceted approach that
included most of the factors in
Mack
that favour a finding of
entrapment, including,

o

The use of trickery, fraud and reward,

o

The use of persistent direction to become more organized, focused

o

The use of persistent veiled threats to adopt the pressure cooker

o

The exploitation of the defendants’ social isolation and desperation

o

The creation of an elaborate ruse that led the defendants to fear

o

The repeated angry encounters with undercover officers who played

o

The decision to play the role of the defendants’ spiritual advisor

•

The police involvement in the offence was
overwhelming compared to the insignificant part played by the defendants;

•

The constant direction and prodding the

the police who were the leaders of this plot;

•

The police took over the leadership and
committed illegal acts to enable the defendants to play their small part in the

•

Mr. Nuttall repeatedly demonstrated that he
lacked the focus required to make the arrangements that were necessary before
the pressure cooker plan could be carried out, even if they had secured the
financial resources required for the mission;

•

The police were exasperated with Mr. Nuttall’s
failure to follow through with any of the extremist objectives he talked about;

•

The police aggressively engineered a plan and
made the defendants think it was their own;

•

The police acts were egregious;

•

There were no exigent circumstances that the
police needed to meet with such extraordinary measures;

•

There was no imminent risk of harm to the public;

•

There was no need to disrupt ongoing criminal
activity;

•

The police were acutely aware that without the
constant supervision and direction of Corporal A., the defendants would be
incapable of completing their part in the plan;

•

The role of the police in the execution of the
plan greatly exceeded the role of the defendants;

•

The police removed all of the defendants’
self-imposed obstacles, as well as the obstacles that the police concluded the
defendants could never overcome because of their vulnerabilities and lack of
resources; and

•

This was not a case where the police learned that
there was a pre-existing plan to carry out a terrorist plot, that steps had
been taken to formulate a terrorist plot, that the defendants were
communicating with known terrorists or terrorist organizations, or that the
defendants possessed any expertise that would have been of value to a terrorist
organization.

[
430
]

The trial judge concluded that the average person, with strengths
and weaknesses, with or without the vulnerabilities of the defendants, would
likely have planted the pressure cooker devices to save their own lives despite
the risk to others. She based her finding on the pressures placed on the
defendants by the police during the undercover operation, as well as the
multi-faceted control the police exerted over their actions and the beliefs.

[
431
]

As explained above, in my view, the trial judge erred in her
conclusion that, objectively, the conduct of the police caused the defendants
to plant the bombs in order to save their lives. If she was correct in that
regard, her conclusion would clearly stand. However, in my respectful view, she
erred, and her error drove her to a conclusion that was wrong in law, just as
the trial judge committed an extricable legal error in
Mack
. The
foundation for her conclusion that the average person would have planted bombs
that would kill many people, with timers set to ensure the deaths or injury of
first responders, falls along with her conclusion that they did so for fear of
their lives.

(4)

Finding that the conduct of the police amounted
to a manufactured crime

[
432
]

However, once again, that is not the end of the issue, as the trial
judge continued with her analysis at paras. 774–780 of her reasons and
found that regardless of the average person test, the conduct of the police in
this case was so egregious that the only conclusion that could be drawn was
that they manufactured the crime and thereby entrapped the defendants,
referring back to the
Mack
analysis where Lamer J. found that even if the hypothetical person would not likely have committed the
offence, the conduct of the police can nevertheless support the conclusion that
they went beyond the bounds of propriety and instigated the crime, and thereby
still amounted to an abuse of process (
Mack
at 961–62).

[
433
]

She continued with her analysis and found that:

•

This was a case of truly manufactured crime by
the RCMP, and not a case where the police simply instigated, originated or
brought about the offence;

•

The police focused their investigation on two
people who held terrorist beliefs but no apparent capacity or means to plan,
act, and carry through with their religiously motivated objectives;

•

The police counselled, directed, urged,
instructed and moulded them into people who, with significant and continuous
supervision and direction by the police, ultimately played a small role in the
terrorist offence;

•

While Mr. Nuttall first identified the
pressure cooker as an explosive device, he wanted to use it as a “tester”, and
the closest he got to an explosive device on his own was to talk about using
cow manure;

•

The police seized on the pressure cooker idea
and it became their plan;

•

The police had to provide the explosive
substance;

•

The police had to take the defendants shopping
and give continuous instructions and direction until they bought what they
needed to make the bombs;

•

The police constructed the device and left the
gluing of the nails and construction of the timers to the defendants;

•

The police had to arrange for a location for the
defendants to work on the devices and provide constant supervision and
direction;

•

The police had to ensure the defendants received
their daily methadone prescription;

•

The police chose the date for the explosion;

•

The police made all of the arrangements for the
accommodation and travel to Victoria;

•

The police chose where the devices would be
planted;

•

The day-to-day dealings with the defendants
demonstrated the “absurd character” of the undercover investigation;

•

Mr. Nuttall broke down after the failed
train plan and said that he was not a general and could not be expected to
create a workable plan;

•

Corporal A. responded by assuring him that he
would be taken through to the end “one baby step at a time”;

•

The police in fact had to take the defendants “one
baby step at a time” to bring the undercover operation to an end with an arrest;

•

The police led the defendants to the end through
manipulation, cajoling, instructing, instillation of fear, offers of friendship,
offers of reward, and offers of religious guidance throughout the operation;
and

•

The police could not continue with an indefinite
undercover operation, but rather than turn the operation back to CSIS, given
there was no imminent risk of criminal activity, they manufactured a crime that
amounted to entrapment.

[
434
]

From the above discussion, it is clear that the trial judge made
some palpable and overriding errors of fact, as well as an error in the
application of the legal principles of entrapment. In my view, the first two
bases upon which she found entrapment, a lack of reasonable suspicion and the
average person test, cannot stand. However, in my view, the trial judge’s third
conclusion is unassailable. This is one of the rare cases that falls outside of
the average person test, but in which the conduct of the police amounts to an
abuse of process in any event.

[
435
]

In
R. v. Lising
,
2010 BCCA 390
, this Court examined the conduct
of a police agent in the context of abuse of process. The Court identified the
two operating factors that require careful balancing: the concepts of fairness
and justice and the need to protect the public from serious crime.

[
436
]

Terrorism
offences are some of the most serious crimes in our law. Unfortunately, Canada
is no stranger to acts of terrorism. The 19th-century assassination of Thomas D’Arcy
McGee, the bombings carried out by the so-called Squamish Five in 1982, and the
bombing of Air India Flight 182 in 1985 are only a few of the violent terrorist
acts that have been perpetrated throughout this country’s history. Terrorists
maim and kill scores of innocent people and threaten the confidence of the
community in their collective security as they go about their day-to-day
activities. There are few crimes so vile, regardless of where in the world they
are committed.

[
437
]

Not all terrorist organizations are as entrenched in their methods
of security and their ability to fend off law enforcement as the Hells Angels were
in
Lising
(see paras.
16–20
). But no doubt some are, and
infiltration of those groups or the gathering of evidence against them could
present almost insurmountable problems and require the police to engage in innovative
and sometimes illegal acts in order to secure the type of evidence necessary
for a prosecution.

[
438
]

On the other hand, the police do not have a free hand to do whatever
they wish in order to investigate crime, even serious crime. The concepts of
fairness and justice are still highly relevant and police conduct undertaken in
the investigation of crime must be balanced against them.

[
439
]

The issue is not whether Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody were
predisposed to commit terrorist acts—clearly they were. It was also flawed
reasoning on the part of the trial judge to suggest that the police were required
to assess their mental health and determine whether they were likely to commit
a terrorist act, because the police could not have been expected to make that
assessment during the throes of this investigation.

[
440
]

However, in this case, the police eventually knew Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody had little to no ability to commit an act of terrorism.
Certainly, they were right to commence the investigation, and certainly they
had reasonable suspicion that the two might commit a crime. However, as found
by the trial judge, the police went far beyond investigating a crime. They
pushed and pushed and pushed the two defendants to come up with a workable
plan. The police did everything necessary to facilitate the plan. I can find no
fault with the trial judge’s conclusion that the police manufactured the crime
that was committed and were the primary actors in its commission. Although in
some cases the police may have to be the primary actor, when all of the circumstances
are considered, assessed, and weighed, the misconduct of the police in this
case far outweighed their violation of the concepts of fairness and justice.

[
441
]

I therefore agree with the trial judge that the overall conduct of
this investigation was a travesty of justice.

[
442
]

This is not to suggest that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody are
harmless. They may be very dangerous. However, that danger was not apparent in
the investigation, which was confirmed by Sergeant K.’s continually telling his
superiors that they presented no imminent danger or risk. There was no danger
because Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody had neither the means nor the
ability to carry out any of the plans without substantial aid from the police.

[
443
]

Thus, I would dismiss the appeal from the stays of proceedings based
on entrapment.

K.

Abuse of Process

[
444
]

The trial judge also performed an independent analysis concluding
that the police conduct also led to an abuse of process. I do not need to
comment on the grounds of appeal as they relate to this conclusion, as I have
already found that her entrapment ruling is not sufficiently tainted by error
to be set aside.

[
445
]

I would add only one thing in relation to her criticism of Corporal
A.’s refusal to find proper spiritual advice for the accused. The evidence overwhelmingly
demonstrates that Mr. Nuttall frequently refused to seek out or adhere to
the beliefs of a moderate imam. His requests for guidance related to whether
killing innocent people, including women and children, as a result of his
violent jihadist acts would be contrary to his religion. He would not take this
inquiry to a moderate imam, and Corporal A. was quite right in his refusal to
take Mr. Nuttall to see an imam who supported violent jihadist acts
instead. The trial judge’s criticism in this regard was unfounded.

L.

Multiple Convictions

[
446
]

The Crown submits that the same analysis of “overlapping counts”
applies to both the Facilitation Count and count 2. I agree that, generally
speaking, the approach set out by the Crown is the proper approach where multiple
convictions overlap. However, every nexus of potentially overlapping offences must
be considered individually.

[
447
]

In my view, the Crown is correct that the trial judge erred in her
analysis of both the Facilitation Count and count 2. Instead, those counts
should have been put to the jury and stayed by the trial judge in accordance
with the procedure in
Kienapple
if overlapping convictions resulted.

(1)

General
approach to overlapping convictions

[
448
]

Before addressing the specific grounds of appeal, the Crown lays out
a framework for what it describes as the “proper procedure for adjudication of
multiple overlapping counts”, which it says also applies to the appeal in
relation to the conspiracy counts. The Crown says that where an indictment
contains multiple counts with overlapping elements, the trial judge must
instruct the jury to deliver verdicts on all counts. If guilty verdicts are
returned, it would then be for the trial judge to determine whether
Kienapple

applies such that conditional stays should be entered on the less serious
overlapping counts.

[
449
]

The Crown says the trial judge failed to follow this procedure in her
rulings on the Facilitation Count and count 2, which prevented the jury from
delivering verdicts on all counts. The Crown submits that both rulings “conflated
the jury’s fact-finding function with the trial judge’s responsibility for
guarding against multiple convictions or double criminality”.

[
450
]

The Crown says it was prejudiced by these rulings by being deprived
of verdicts on the Facilitation Count and on count 2. It says that if the jury’s
verdict on count 1 was set aside on appeal, then the Crown would be precluded
from arguing that convictions should be entered on these counts since the jury
never returned verdicts on them.

[
451
]

The respondents provide a functional response to the Crown’s
prejudice submissions: they are not appealing their convictions, so the Crown’s
theory of prejudice could never materialize. They further submit that the Crown
erroneously attempts to characterize the trial judge’s rulings as
misapplications of the
Kienapple
principle. In reality, the respondents
say that the rulings are, respectively, applications of the substantive law of
conspiracy and statutory interpretation of the elements of s. 83.19 of the

Code
, which neither attract the
Kienapple
principle nor contain
other reversible errors.

[
452
]

I agree with the defence that the trial judge’s decisions were
procedurally prior to any consideration of the
Kienapple
principle. The
Kienapple

principle is applied by a trial judge when she would otherwise enter
convictions for multiple offences arising from the same delict. It does not
deprive the trial judge of the ability or the obligation to perform statutory
interpretation to determine the elements of an offence in the
Code
and
to take counts away from the jury if necessary. Nor does it prevent a judge
from severing counts from an indictment where appropriate.

[
453
]

Thus, if the trial judge’s rulings were correct, there would be no
need to resort to the
Kienapple
principle. However, for the reasons that
follow, I agree with the Crown that both of the trial judge’s rulings were
incorrect. Had she resolved those issues correctly, both counts that she took
away from the jury would have attracted the
Kienapple
principle if the
jury rendered guilty verdicts.

(2)

Directed
verdict on the Facilitation Count

[
454
]

The trial judge directed a verdict of not guilty on count 3 of the
indictment in relation to the charge of facilitating a terrorist offence. Her reasons
are summarized above.

[
455
]

The Facilitation Count charged the accused with
an offence under s. 83.19 of the
Code
:

Between the 1
st
day of February,
2013 and the 2
nd
day of July, 2013, at or near the Cities of Surrey
and Victoria, British Columbia and elsewhere in the Province of British
Columbia did knowingly facilitate a terrorist activity, thereby committing an
offence contrary to
section 83.19
of the
Criminal Code
.

[
456
]

The Facilitation Count was particularized as follows:

Ms. Korody and
Mr. Nuttall facilitated a terrorist activity, to wit, the placing of an
explosive device in or against the British Columbia Parliament building
grounds, Victoria, British Columbia, a place of public use and a government or
public facility, with intent to cause death or serious bodily injury.

[
457
]

Section 83.19 of the
Code
reads:

83.19 (1) Every one
who knowingly facilitates a terrorist activity is guilty of an indictable
offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

(2) For the purposes of this Part, a
terrorist activity is facilitated whether or not

(a) the facilitator
knows that a particular terrorist activity is facilitated;

(b) any particular
terrorist activity was foreseen or planned at the time it was facilitated; or

(c) any terrorist activity was actually carried out.

[
458
]

The trial judge determined that the purpose of
s. 83.19 of the
Code
was “to capture persons who were on the
periphery of terrorist groups and activities, but nevertheless aided in
carrying out the acts themselves”. Thus,
she
concluded that the conduct targeted by s. 83.19 of the
Code
was not
encompassed by the evidence led by the Crown and was inconsistent with the
theory of liability it maintained throughout its case. Accordingly, she
directed a verdict of not guilty for both accused on the Facilitation Count.

a.

Positions of the parties

[
459
]

The Crown submits that although its theory at trial was that the
accused were principals, its theory should not have been the sole or
determinative factor in the trial judge’s directed verdict ruling. The Crown
says the defence position was also relevant. The Crown says that since the
defence position was that the Crown failed to prove any completed offences, the
Facilitation Count should have been left with the jury for it to decide
whether, even if the accused’s conduct did not involve completed terrorist
offences, it still amounted to facilitation of terrorist activity. According to
the Crown, because the trier of fact is not bound by the parties’ theories, the
Facilitation Count should have been left to the jury to decide in light of the
allegations in the indictment and the evidence adduced at trial. As laid out
above, any concerns about double punishment in light of overlapping
convictions, says the Crown, should have been addressed through the
Kienapple

principle after the jury delivered their verdicts on all counts.

[
460
]

The respondents’ position is that the Crown’s argument on appeal
misses the central point of the trial judge’s ruling. They say that her ruling
was a straightforward no-evidence ruling along the following lines: she
determined that a necessary element of s. 83.19 of the
Code
was the
commission of an act that made it easier for
another person
to commit a
terrorist act, and that the Crown led no evidence speaking to that element of
the offence. The Facilitation Count therefore could not go to the jury. The
respondents say the Crown’s particulars made it clear that the alleged “facilitation”
was the placing of the devices at the Parliament Buildings, and they submit
that there was no evidence suggesting they aided anyone else to do so.

[
461
]

Additionally, the respondents say that any defence theories of
liability should play no part in a directed verdict application, because the
defence position on any count in the indictment “is only imperfectly known, if
it is known at all, at the time a directed verdict application is heard”.

[
462
]

In reply to the Crown argument that the jury could have acquitted
the accused of the “completed terrorism offences” but still convicted on the
Facilitation Count, the respondents say that it is inaccurate to refer to a
conspiracy charge in such terms, as a conspiracy is inchoate and does not
involve the “completion” of another offence. Additionally, the respondents
refer back to the foundational premise of the trial judge’s directed verdict—that
the Crown led no evidence that the accused assisted
any other person’s

terrorist activity, which she found to be essential to convict under s. 83.19
of the
Code
.

[
463
]

Finally, the respondents say that, in any event, the trial judge’s
entrapment ruling would necessarily also apply to the Facilitation Count even
if the trial judge did err in directing a verdict of not guilty.

b.

Discussion

[
464
]

Before I commence the discussion of the issue at hand, I find it
necessary to comment on the needless complexity of the legislation that
comprises Part II.1 of the
Code
. It would be beneficial if Parliament
revisited the legislation, revamped it, and made it comprehensible,
particularly for those members of the public who sit as jury members on such
cases.

[
465
]

As noted above, the trial judge gave comprehensive reasons for
concluding that the Facilitation Count should be withdrawn from the jury. Her
reasoning has been followed by Justice David in
R. c. Jamali
,

2017 QCCS 6078
at paras.
43–57
.

[
466
]

In my view, the trial judge proceeded on an incorrect
premise when she stated, at para. 95 of her reasons, that “…the
particulars describe the facilitation as the placing of explosive devices on
the legislative grounds”. That is not how the offence was particularized. For
convenience, I repeat the particulars of the count:

Ms. Korody and Mr. Nuttall facilitated a terrorist activity,
to
wit
, the placing of an explosive device in or against the British Columbia
Parliament building grounds, Victoria, British Columbia, a place of public use
and a government or public facility, with intent to cause death or serious
bodily injury.

[Emphasis added.]

[
467
]

If the particulars said that the respondents facilitated a terrorist
activity
by
placing the devices at the Parliament Buildings, I would
agree that the facilitating offence was limited to the act of placing the
explosive devices. However, the particulars say that the terrorist activity was
placing the devices at the Parliament Buildings. It is that activity that was facilitated,
which is made clear by the use of the descriptor “to wit” in the particulars.
Thus, the acts of buying the pressure cookers and other materials, the acts of
scouting out suitable targets, and all other acts in preparation could amount
to facilitating that activity.

[
468
]

I agree with the trial judge that in this context, the definition
found in
Lindsay

is the applicable
definition: “to make a matter easier”, and as “the act of making it easier for
another person to commit a crime”:
Lindsay

at paras.
23 and 24
.

[
469
]

The meaning of the word “facilitate”, in
the context of s. 83.19, includes making it easier for another person to
bring about a terrorist activity. The criminal organization legislation bears
many similarities to the terrorism legislation and provides a useful comparator.
Multiple parties can do far more harm acting in concert than they can separately.
This is of particular importance in both the criminal organization and
terrorism contexts. However, I am not convinced that in all cases the
definition is limited to facilitating “another” person.

[
470
]

Child luring legislation also contains “facilitation”.
In
R. v. Legare
,

2009 SCC 56
, a similar
definition was used at para. 28 that “facilitate” means helping to bring
about, making easier or more probable.
Legare
involved s. 172.1:
using telecommunication to communicate with a young child for the purpose of
facilitating a specified sexual offence. As
noted in
Legare

at para.
25
,
facilitation is an inchoate offence done in preparation of the actual crime,
even preceding an attempt to commit that crime. The same may hold true for
facilitating a terrorist activity:
R. v. Khawaja
,
2012 SCC 69
at paras.
57–63
.

In
Legare
, an accused could be both the principal and the facilitator. However,
in s. 172.1, the offence was
communicating
for the purpose of
facilitation. Here, the offence is actual facilitation of a terrorist activity.
It is clear from the subject matter of s. 172.1 that the provision contemplates
communication with the eventual victim of the facilitated offence by a perpetrator
who will often act alone. It is an example where “facilitate” applies to being
able to facilitate oneself.

[
471
]

I agree with the trial judge that the purpose of the facilitation
offence is to capture those on the periphery of terrorist groups and
activities. Indeed, the section ensures that facilitators excluded by virtue of
the intent requirements of the party liability provisions in s. 21 of the
Code

are nevertheless captured under s. 83.19. However, I do not conclude that
the section is limited to those on the periphery. While I agree that a person
cannot be convicted as a principal and a facilitator of the same terrorist
activity, one could be
charged
as a principal and a facilitator, just as
one could be
charged
, but not convicted, as both a principal and an
aider, abettor, or accessory after the fact.

[
472
]

I agree with the defence that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody could
not facilitate their own completed activity. I agree that the elements of the
offence of facilitation, by its definition, generally include facilitating
another person to commit a terrorist activity. However, in circumstances such
as these, in which multiple individuals allegedly carried out a terrorist
activity in concert, depending on the evidence, each could facilitate the act
of the other.

[
473
]

I also do not wish to foreclose the possibility of an accused
facilitating themselves. There may be a case where the facts fall short of a
completed offence, or even an attempt to commit a terrorist act by one person,
but that person could have taken sufficient steps towards committing the act to
be found to have facilitated a terrorist activity.

[
474
]

Thus, in the context of this case, the trial judge should not have
directed a verdict of not guilty on the Facilitation Count, and should have
instead left it with the jury to decide whether Ms. Korody facilitated Mr. Nuttall
or vice versa. If the jury returned a guilty verdict on all counts, the trial
judge would then have applied the principles in
Kienapple
to address any
issue in relation to double jeopardy or double criminality. The defence
position at trial was that the offences were not completed. The nature of what Mr. Nuttall
and Ms. Korody were planning changed constantly. If the jury accepted that
submission, and acquitted one or the other on the conspiracy counts, there could
still be evidence to support the Facilitation Count.

[
475
]

The next question is what remedy should flow from this error. The
jury convicted both accused on count 1: conspiracy to commit murder. Therefore,
a guilty verdict on the Facilitation Count would have been conditionally stayed
by the application of the
Kienapple
principle. The verdict would also be
subject to a stay of proceedings based on the entrapment finding.

[
476
]

This Court derives its power to allow or dismiss a Crown appeal in a
criminal case from s. 686(4) of the
Code
. Under ordinary
circumstances, the Crown would be entitled to a new trial on the Facilitation Count.
The Crown sought a new trial but requested that the order for a new trial be
conditionally stayed, depending on the outcome of the entrapment appeal.

[
477
]

When exercising its powers under s. 686(4) of the
Code
,
s. 686(8) allows a court of appeal to make any additional order that
justice requires. This Court has the residual discretion under that section to
stay a charge where further proceedings would constitute an abuse of process:
R.
v. Hinse
,
1995 CanLII 54 (SCC)
, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 597 at para.
23
. Given that the entrapment
argument was upheld on appeal, any further proceedings would constitute an
abuse of process.

[
478
]

The proper course of action is to allow the appeal under s. 686(4)(b)(i),
but to substitute a stay of proceedings on the basis that the respondents were
entrapped and any further proceedings would therefore be abusive.

(3)

Ruling
on the duplicity of counts 1 and 2

[
479
]

The defence also applied for a ruling that counts 1 and 2 of the
indictment, which both deal with conspiracy, were duplicitous because they both
related to the same agreement and merely represented two objects of the same
conspiracy.

[
480
]

The operative part of count 1 reads that the
accused:

…did conspire together, the one with the
other, to murder persons unknown contrary to
s.465(1)
(a) of the
Criminal
Code
,

for the benefit of, at the direction of, or in association
with a terrorist group…

[
481
]

The operative part of count 2 reads that the accused:

…did conspire together, the one with the
other, to commit an indictable offence, to wit: placing an explosive in or
against a place of public use, or a government or public facility, with intent
to cause death or serious bodily injury, contrary to
s.431.2(2)
of the
Criminal
Code
,

for the benefit of, at the direction or, or in association
with a terrorist group…

[
482
]

Although the Crown did not particularize either count, it limited
its case on both counts to a conspiracy to place the pressure cooker devices on
the grounds of the Parliament Buildings in Victoria.

[
483
]

The trial judge noted that the sole difference between these two counts
is the object of the conspiracy, in that the second count includes an intention
to cause serious bodily injury as an alternative to an intention to cause
death.

[
484
]

The trial judge held that where there is only one agreement, but
different illegal objects, there can only be one conspiracy conviction, because
the “substance of the offence of conspiracy to commit an indictable offence is
the agreement and not the commission of the offence”. She noted that where a
single conspiracy has multiple objects, the Crown need only prove one object to
support a conviction.

[
485
]

The trial judge determined that if the jury were to convict on count
1, it should not go on to determine if the accused were guilty on count 2. She decided
that she would remedy the duplicity in the counts by giving an instruction to
that effect to the jury. Because the jury ultimately convicted the accused on count
1, it did not return a verdict on count 2. The trial judge entered a conditional
stay of proceedings on that count, and later deleted the conditional aspect of
the stay.

a.

Positions of the parties

[
486
]

The core of the Crown’s argument on this ground of appeal is that
the proper procedure for the trial judge to follow would have been to require
the jury to deliver verdicts on every count in the indictment and subsequently
apply the
Kienapple
principle to avoid double punishment. It says that
if the verdict on count 1 were set aside on appeal, the trial judge’s ruling would
deprive the Crown of the opportunity to argue for a conviction on count 2.
While there may be considerable overlap between the two counts, the Crown
argues that their legal elements were not identical, and the accused could have
the requisite
mens rea
to place bombs with intent to cause serious
bodily harm without having an intent to cause death.

[
487
]

The Crown says that multiple counts arising out of the same incident
are not duplicitous, “even where they may overlap or duplicate each other”.
Thus, the trial judge should have directed the jury to deliver verdicts on all counts
and then decide whether to conditionally stay some of them by applying the
Kienapple

principle.

[
488
]

The respondent first notes that the trial Crown (who is not counsel
on appeal) took a different position in the court below, where the Crown submitted
that count 1 and count 2 were two legally distinct conspiracies, such that, even
on an application of
Kienapple
, the jury could convict on both.

[
489
]

In response to the Crown’s appeal submissions, the respondents say
that conspiracy jurisprudence establishes that “where a criminal agreement has
multiple unlawful objects, there is nonetheless just a single conspiracy”, and
that the Crown need only prove an agreement to carry out one unlawful object to
convict.

[
490
]

The respondents submit that the
Kienapple
principle, which
addresses a situation in which a single delict is the basis for charges under
multiple
Code
provisions, is inapplicable to conspiracy charges. The
respondents provide two examples to illustrate that the Crown suffered no
prejudice from the trial judge’s declining to address the ruling through the
Kienapple

framework. If, as the Crown suggests, the jury delivered verdicts on all counts,
with guilty verdicts on both conspiracy counts, there could only be two
possible outcomes:

(i)

If the trial judge entered a conditional stay on
one count based on
Kienapple
, the Crown would be in the same position on
appeal as it already is, demonstrating that no prejudice flowed from the trial
judge’s declining to address the ruling through the
Kienapple
framework;
or

(ii)

If the trial judge decided that the
Kienapple

test was not met, the accused would be convicted twice for the same
conspiracy, leading to a successful defence appeal.

[
491
]

In example (i), the respondents say that there was no route to a
successful Crown appeal from the trial judge’s conditional stay of one of the
conspiracy counts, because their argument presupposes that this was a situation
where the laying of two counts was legally sound, as is the case in the usual
situation where
Kienapple
arises; no legal principles forbid an
indictment charging counts with overlapping elements, and
Kienapple
merely
ensures no unfairness in the result. They submit that legal principles do
prohibit, however, an indictment charging the same conspiracy twice.

[
492
]

The respondents also submit that any alleged prejudice the Crown
suffered is meaningless because they did not appeal any of their convictions.
Finally, they say that the trial judge’s entrapment ruling also applies to count
2, even if a jury had delivered a verdict on that count.

b.

Discussion

[
493
]

The defence submits that
Kienapple
has no application to
conspiracy, citing
Cox and Paton v. The Queen
,
1963 CanLII 78 (SCC)
, [1963] S.C.R. 500. That
case determined that if there is one agreement, there is only one conspiracy.
This does not mean, however, that the same agreement cannot be charged with
different objects if the Crown is concerned about whether it can prove one of
those objects.

[
494
]

The problem arises in this case because of the wildly different
positions taken by the respondents in terms of what they were agreeing to
during the investigation. While in hindsight, it would have been far better had
the Crown not cluttered the indictment by laying two counts and had only
proceeded with count 2, it appears that the Crown at trial was of the view that
each count represented a separate conspiracy. That position has been withdrawn
on appeal. Given that the jury could have accepted all, part, or none of a
witness’s testimony, there was a route to an acquittal on count 1 and a
conviction on count 2. In this case, had there been a successful appeal on
count 1, count 2 would not be available as a substitute because the jury did
not return a verdict.

[
495
]

Prior to
R. v. Provo
,
1989 CanLII 71 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 3, judges who applied
the
Kienapple
principle sometimes entered acquittals on the overlapping count
or directed juries to deal with the overlapping count by either acquitting or
not considering a count depending on its finding on another. That is the
approach the trial judge took here. In
Provo
, the Court set out the
appropriate process for considering overlapping offences and concluded that the
best approach would be for the trial judge to enter a conditional stay of
proceedings on the lesser offence if the jury convicted the accused of both, thus
preserving the guilty verdict on the lesser offence in case of an appeal. Thus,
the Crown would not be obliged to appeal the stay (as it was here). If the
conviction on the main count was either not appealed or affirmed on appeal, the
conditional nature of the stay would become permanent.

[
496
]

In this case, because there were different objects alleged, the
trial judge should have left both offences with the jury and then, if guilty
verdicts were rendered on each count, engaged in the application of the
Kienapple

principle and recorded a conviction for only the more serious offence, the
conspiracy to commit murder. She would then have entered a conditional stay on count
2: see
Ontario (Ministry of Labour) v. Black & McDonald Ltd.
,
2011
ONCA 440
.

[
497
]

As the Crown conceded, this conclusion makes little difference, as
the result would be the same: a stay of proceedings on count 2 entered by this
Court, on the basis of either
Kienapple
or entrapment.

[
498
]

It is well established that on an appeal from an acquittal on a question
of law, the Crown must demonstrate both that an error of law was made, and that
there is a reasonable degree of certainty that but for the error, the result
would not necessarily have been the same:
Cullen v. The King
,
1949 CanLII 7 (SCC)
, [1949]
S.C.R. 658 at 665;
R. v. Morin
,
1988 CanLII 8 (SCC)
, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 345 at 374;
R. v.
Graveline
,
2006 SCC 16
at paras.
14–16
.

[
499
]

In my view, there is no reason to limit this principle to Crown
appeals from acquittals on questions of law. The Crown was limited to appeals
on this narrow basis until 1985, when Crown appeals were broadened to include
appeals from stays of proceedings and quashed indictments:
Criminal Law
Amendment, 1985
, R.S. 1985, c. 27 (1st Supp.), s. 139. But even before
the 1985 amendment came into effect, the Crown could appeal from stays of
proceedings as though they were acquittals:
R. v. Jewitt
,
1985 CanLII 47 (SCC)
, [1985] 2
S.C.R. 128.

[
500
]

When the Crown appeals from a stay of proceedings, it must therefore
establish that the stay was incorrectly entered, and must also satisfy the
court that there is some real likelihood that the result would have been
different. If there is no real prospect of a different result, then the Crown
has not discharged its burden and the accused cannot be retried.

[
501
]

Here, the result remains a stay of proceedings. Thus, I would dismiss
this appeal.

M.

Conclusion

[
502
]

In summary, I conclude that the trial judge did not err in finding
that Mr. Nuttall and Ms. Korody were entrapped and in entering a stay
of proceedings. I would dismiss the appeal from the stays of proceedings
entered on counts 1 and 4.

[
503
]

I conclude that the trial judge erred when she removed the
Facilitation Count from the jury. I would allow the appeal on count 3 to the
extent of setting aside the acquittal and substituting a stay of proceedings on
the basis that a new trial would be an abuse of process.

[
504
]

Finally, I conclude that the trial judge also erred in instructing
the jury not to consider count 2 if it convicted on count 1. I would, however,
dismiss the appeal from the stay of proceedings she entered. If the jury had
rendered a guilty verdict on count 2, a stay of proceedings would be the
result.
